teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule of deliberate action used as a lever in courtship: if the great think before they promise, a lover who swore cannot later plead haste, so the maxim becomes a way to bind a promise.

note: In 61 the friend tells the woman not to grieve gazing at the wall scored with the days; in 289 the man on the road imagines her looking at that wall.
teaches: The wall marked with the days of absence was known to both sides of the parting: the man can picture the very ritual the friend tries to stop, so his guilt in 289 rests on a convention the woman's side also names.

note: Purananuru 48 says Thondi smells of the neythal flowers blooming in its great backwater; Akananuru 290 says the woman's eyes were once like the great cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour.
teaches: Thondi's neythal was the town's own emblem in praise of its king, so when the akam poet says her eyes have lost that likeness he is measuring her pallor against a flower the audience knew as Thondi's pride.

note: Both are Mamoolanar's: in 61 the man would not stay even for Pulli's festive Venkadam; in 295 he has gone past Pulli's hill into the Vadugar country where the language changes.
teaches: Read together, the poet's Pulli's hill is the last familiar landmark: one poem stops at it as the measure of a great prize, the other goes beyond it to a land of strange speech, giving his geography of absence an inner and an outer edge.

note: Both are marutham poems in which the friend refuses the husband and compares the gossip about him to noise at Chezhiyan's Koodal; in 116 it is louder than the shout of the battlefield where he routed two kings, in 296 it is like the city's everyday clamour.
teaches: The akam poets measured scandal by the noise of the Pandya capital in war and in peace alike, so Koodal's fame worked as a ready scale for how far gossip had spread.

note: Purananuru 264 tells of a hero-stone newly set up with his name engraved and crowned with a peacock feather; Akananuru 297 shows such a stone grown old, its inscribed name passed unread by weary travellers.
teaches: The puram poem records the moment a name is carved to outlast death, and the akam poem shows the same kind of stone generations on with no one reading it, so the pair qualifies the promise of the engraved name.

note: Both use the wandering kodiyar troupe: in 301 their leaving empties a town's commons, and that emptiness is the heroine's evening; in 309 their going to Vaanavan is the model for the heroine's own journey after her man.
teaches: The same performers figure both sides of parting, the place left desolate and the traveller who will not count the forest long, so akam poets used the bards' life as a ready picture of both staying and going.

note: Akananuru 303 calls Paari the giver of hill-like elephants to any suppliant and makes his Parambu the place sparrows always return to at evening; Purananuru 108 says Paari never answers a suppliant with 'I will not come'.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the certainty of Paari's giving, famous from the puram poems, to make the sparrows' return seem certain, so that the heroine's disappointment is measured against a patron who never failed anyone.

note: Both open in the first rains with a stag, a doe and her fawn together; in 304 the hero sees them from the war camp and imagines his wife's reproach, in 314 the friend sees them as the hero comes home in time.
teaches: One scene of the deer family carries reproach while he is away and fulfilment when he returns, which shows that what a karu thing implies is fixed by the uri of the poem, not by the thing itself.

note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

note: The same poet, Maruthan Ilanagan, praises Vazhuthi's war in Purananuru 52 and in Akananuru 312 likens lightning to the spear Vazhuthi raises against fleeing enemies.
teaches: One poet's war praise for a Pandya becomes, in his love poem, the measure of a storm's power, showing puram fame travelling into akam as a simile that its first hearers would recognise.

note: Both describe the waterless road where bowmen shoot travellers and birds feed on the dead; in Purananuru 3 suppliants brave it for the Pandya's gifts, in Akananuru 313 the husband crosses it for wealth.
teaches: The same death road is crossed for the same motive, gain, by the suppliant and by the husband; puram counts the crossing as praise of the patron, akam as the measure of what the wife fears.

note: Both are the friend telling the wife not to prolong her sulking: Kural 1302 says sulking is salt and too much spoils it; Akananuru 316 shows women who sulked too long left alone, poor and nursing hungry sons.
teaches: What the Kural calls spoiling by too much salt the Sangam friend spells out as the loss of fortune and household, so the couplet's measured image stands for a social and economic ruin, not only a lost pleasure.

note: Both are the friend turning back a man who comes at night by a beast-haunted hill path: in 308 she offers day meetings instead, in 318 she bans his visits and offers marriage.
teaches: Read in order, the two refusals show the stages of the friend's pressure: first moving the meeting to day, still within secret love, then closing the meetings so that marriage is the only road left.

note: Both are spoken to a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell me if you are not going, and keep your promise of a quick return for those who will still be alive; Akananuru 319's friend says go and get your wealth, since the girl cannot even say she will stay behind.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows why the friend speaks in this situation at all: the girl is too young and loving to answer him herself, which supports reading the couplet's 'tell me' as the friend speaking for her.

note: 326 likens the young woman's unerring eyes to the spear raised by Pazhaiyan, lord of Por and the Cholas' champion; 44 recalls the battle in which Pazhaiyan fell (பழையன் பட்டென) and Chenni avenged him.
teaches: Akam poets drew on both halves of one champion's story, his unfailing aim for a woman's dangerous eyes and his death for the scale of a war that keeps a husband from home, so the hero's fame served love poetry whole.

note: Both are marutham speeches by a courtesan meant for the hearing of others, and both stake her bangles on Chola martial formulas: 186 says the lord never broke her bangles, using Pazhaiyan's 'rain of arrows, cloud-dark shields' (மாரி அம்பின் மழைத்தோல்); 336 applies the same phrase to the Cholas and curses her bangles to break like the Aryans at Vallam.
teaches: The pair shows the courtesan's boast as a set form: her bangles stand for her hold on the man, and she guarantees them with the same Chola war formula, as a warrior swears by his king.

note: 338 wishes love to last like the Porai's Kolli; 209 tells how Kari killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras, who set a goddess image there.
teaches: Read with 209, the hero's figure of permanence is a hill that changed lords by a killing, so what the poet makes lasting is the hill itself, not any house that held it.

note: Purananuru 158 names Kolli as the hill Ori ruled, among seven givers now dead; Akananuru 338 calls Kolli the Porai's and makes it the measure of a love that must not perish.
teaches: The puram poem remembers Kolli by a dead patron and the akam poem by its new Chera master, so the hill a lover swears by already carries the record of a fallen lord.

note: Both name Thithiyan as lord of Pothiyil: 25 has his drums echoed in the waterfalls of the hills the absent man crossed; 322 makes his guarded, honey-hung peak the measure of how hard the girl is to reach.
teaches: One chief's hill serves two opposite uses, the distance a husband has gone and the closeness a lover cannot reach, which shows akam poets taking a puram place for its fit to the speaker's situation, not for its praise.

note: Both poems in this chapter name Thithiyan: 322 his war elephants and his guarded Pothiyil; 331 his daily court, his gifts to bards and the sword he drew against the Velir.
teaches: The same patron lends the frustrated lover his inaccessible hill and the abandoned wife his sword, so each speaker takes from a king's fame the face that matches her or his own trouble.

note: 85 names Thiraiyan's Venkatam hill on the road the husband crossed; 340 names Thiraiyan's flowery seaside town Pavaththiri as the measure of the girl's beauty.
teaches: The same chief furnishes a mountain for a paalai poem and a shore town for a neythal one, so a patron's domain was divided among the landscapes as the thinai required.

note: Same thurai: a man, his task done, urges his charioteer home. 34 drives by the stag that feeds and guards its doe; 334 by the breaking rains, hail and peacocks, and by the tribute won with the war drum.
teaches: Together they show the homecoming poem built in two ways: by a creature whose care mirrors the husband's intent (34), or by the season itself whose arrival is the pledge kept (334).

note: Both are night-tryst poems the lover overhears, and both close on the same formula, a tusker and his mate asleep on the plantain slope (வாழையஞ் சிலம்பிற் றுஞ்சும் / வாழையம் சிலம்பில் துஞ்சும்): in 328 he strokes a mate who has just calved, in 332 he lies down with her after killing a tiger.
teaches: A shared formula takes a different act each time to suit the speech: the calving mate presses toward married life in a poem of fear, the tiger-killing protector confirms the lover in a poem of praise.

note: Both are men arguing with hearts set on wealth, and both make the desert's killers the argument: in 327 the archers pity no victim and grieve only when they miss; in 337 the Mazhavar kill a starving messenger in case he has gold and leave scorning his rags.
teaches: Side by side they show the road weighing a man's life only by what he might carry, which is the very reckoning the heart is making when it trades her company for wealth.

note: Kural 1124: she is living to my life when with me and dying when she leaves; Akananuru 339 ends with love like the life's living and parting like dying, spoken by a husband as he sets out.
teaches: The Kural says it in courtship as praise; the poem puts the same claim in the mouth of a man choosing to leave, so the saying becomes the cost he knowingly pays, burning at both ends of the firebrand.

note: Kural 1122 calls the bond with the girl that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை ... நட்பு); 339 has the same word and image, friendship like life joined to the body (யாக்கைக்கு உயிர்இயைந் தன்ன நட்பின்).
teaches: The shared image and even the shared word நட்பு show the Kural's couplet as a distilled form of an akam figure that the poem still spends a scene of departure to earn.

note: Kural 247 grants that this world is not for those without wealth; Akananuru 335 opens by conceding that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, then gives up the journey for wealth anyway.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's premise about wealth in so many words yet refuses its practical pull, showing that the premise alone did not settle whether a husband should leave home to earn.

note: Kural 629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain; Akananuru 327 tells the heart that joy and grief come by turns like day and night, so it need not go seeking hardship for wealth.
teaches: The same doctrine of joy and grief in turn, which the Kural uses to teach calm under misfortune, becomes in the lover's mouth an argument for staying home rather than chasing gain.

note: Kural 81: all of keeping house is for receiving guests; in Akananuru 324 the attendants announce the husband's return by saying his wife will now have guests to feed too.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule from the inside of an absence: hospitality belonged to the couple, so a wife alone could not host, and the husband's return is announced as the return of guests.

note: Both are mullai poems in which the hero, his work done, tells the charioteer to drive fast through the rain-fed forest to his waiting wife.
teaches: Akananuru 34 grounds the hurry in an animal pair (the stag feeding and guarding his doe) while 344 grounds it in the clock, before evening falls, so the homecoming formula could be driven either by an emblem of care or by the promised hour.

note: Both are mullai homecomings after the task: in 344 the hero urges his charioteer; in 354 the attendants urge the hero, naming the victory and the cowherds' evening.
teaches: The pair shows the same return from both ends of command: the hero who orders speed in 344 is himself ordered by his men in 354, and both make the wife's pallor the thing his arrival cures.

note: Both poems by Mamoolanar use Cheralathan, who drove back the sea and cut the kadambu: 127 his tribute treasure, 347 his drum.
teaches: One poet drew two different measures from a single Chera victory, its plunder as the scale of the wealth the husband will not stay for and its drum as the scale of the gossip's noise, so akam borrowed puram events for value and for loudness alike.

note: Both paalai poems pass through the country of Ezhil hill: 345 recalls it as the hill sung by a poet given horses, 349 as Nannan's land where bards are given wealth unasked.
teaches: Read together they show that Ezhil hill was known through its patron's gifts to poets, so the absent husband's road ran through a landscape whose fame was generosity, sharpening the contrast with the man who left home to get wealth.

note: The Kural's woman has worn her fingers marking the days since he left; 351 names the marks drawn on the wall that she counts each day.
teaches: The couplet speaks only from the woman's side, while 351 puts the same tally marks in the returning man's mind, so the counting of days on the wall was a known practice that both partners could picture, not a private secret of the one who waits.

note: Both start from the coming of age: the Naladiyar's wise renounce early because grey hair will come; 353's hero refuses to leave his wife because the days pass like a dream and age is coming.
teaches: The same premise, that youth is short, yields opposite counsels, renunciation in the Naladiyar and staying in married love in 353, so impermanence was a shared starting point that the akam poets turned toward the household and the didactic poets away from it.

note: Both are spoken by the hero to his heart about the journey for wealth: 351 as he returns with it, 353 when the heart at home urges a second journey.
teaches: Placed in sequence the two show the pull of wealth outlasting its success: the heart that raced home in 351 is restless again in 353, and only the argument from age and the wife's virtue holds it back.

note: Both are the man at the king's war: the couplet wishes the king victory so that he may join his wife for the evening feast; in 354 the king has won and raised his flag, and the attendants urge the hero home before her pallor deepens.
teaches: The couplet's wish has two conditions, the king's victory and the evening at home, and 354 shows them met in order (the flag raised, the herds coming in at dusk), so the Kural's line compresses a whole mullai homecoming whose hinge is that the hero's private return waits on the public war.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Both are neythal poems in which the friend answers a lover's daytime visit at dusk: 350 asks him to stay and points to the town, 360 refuses the day meeting and sets a secret night one.
teaches: At the same hour the friend has two opposite tactics, drawing the lover openly toward the village in 350 and hiding him by night in 360, so the dusk scene of neythal could press either toward marriage or toward deeper secrecy.

note: Both open on the spring signs of new leaves and the koel calling in the mango and set them against the man's absence.
teaches: The same signs bring helpless lament in 341 ('there is no way through') and a planned reproach in 355 (we will go and quarrel with him), so the season's cue fixed the occasion but not the heroine's response.

note: Both make the man say that the sweetest thing is an embrace that lets nothing come between: in the Kural not even a breeze, in the poem not even a thread, at which she sulks.
teaches: The couplet states the delight as settled, while the poem quotes it as the argument the man lost to his heart's desire for wealth, so the Kural's claim is shown being tested and overruled inside the paalai situation.

note: Both are the hero's words to his heart under the same occasion (அல்ல குறி), both liken the girl to the treasure the old Velir guarded at Pazhi, and both turn on எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய்.
teaches: The repeated opening under one thurai shows a fixed formula for the spoiled night meeting, the Velir's hidden gold at Pazhi standing for the guarded girl, which 258 then ends in the heart's ruin and 372 in a run of similes for its swinging.

note: Pazhi is the Velir's god-guarded treasure city in 372 and the copper-walled fort Ilamperunchenni broke in 375.
teaches: One fort served akam poets for both halves of its story, as the byword for what cannot be reached and as the scene of a famous breach, so a puram place-name carried opposite meanings depending on which part of its history the speaker needed.

note: Kazhuvul's Kaamur is a place of blessed vengai fragrance in 365 and the town thrown into turmoil by the fourteen Velir in 135.
teaches: The same chieftain's town gives one poet the image of calm sweetness for the wife's hair and another the image of a besieged, shaken heart, showing that a puram name entered akam with its whole history, peace and siege alike, available for comparison.
audit_text_issue: 365 lines 7-8 are hard to construe.

note: Evvi is the unsparing giver (ஓம்பா ஈகை மாவேள் எவ்வி) in the Purananuru poem and the lord who gives toddy to the fishermen to end a brawl in 366.
teaches: The Purananuru names Evvi's giving as a title, while the akam simile shows it as a scene of keeping peace between farmers and salt-makers and makes his shade a measure of a woman's comfort, so a patron's fame for protection became an akam image of shelter.

note: Both use the figure of the ஓர்எயில் மன்னன, the chieftain of a single fort set against crowned kings: in 338 he will not give his daughter to them, in 373 he lies sleepless under their siege.
teaches: The kaanchi poem on a daughter refused to kings shows where the akam poet's image came from: the lone fort's siege was a known situation of puram, and the akam poet borrowed only its sleepless watch to picture the wife.

note: Both are a courtesan's words to the man, both liken his loss to the Kaveri seizing and hiding Atthi, and both end on the demand to give back her beauty and go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே).
teaches: Two poems sharing speaker, legend and closing line show that the Atthi story and the 'return my beauty' demand formed a stock courtesan's reproach, which each poet then fitted to a different king's town as the measure of her lost beauty.

note: Karikal is the victor of Venni in the Purananuru poem and the onlooker at Atthi's flood-dance at Kazhar in 376.
teaches: The conqueror praised in puram appears in akam only as a royal spectator who dates and places a love legend, so akam poets used a war king's fame as a frame for a story of loss rather than of victory.
audit_text_issue: 376 lines 1-2 are compressed.

note: The Kural says to give and live with renown (இசைபட) as the only gain; the poem names those who give with renown (இசைபடப் பெய்தல்) as the men who must sleep in ruined halls on the road to wealth.
teaches: The poem shows what the Kural's rule costs a married man: renown from giving needs wealth, and wealth needs the wasteland and separation, so the maxim's single profit is bought with the akam hero's loneliness.

note: Both say great wealth does not last: the Kural likens its coming and going to a crowd at a dance hall, the poem likens its passing to a night's dream.
teaches: The poem turns the Kural's general warning about wealth into a reason for a husband to stay home, using impermanence not to urge giving but to set the wife's embrace above a second journey for gain.

note: Both are a mother's words after the daughter's elopement; in 15 the mother prays that the town the girl reaches be rich and welcoming to strangers, in 369 the foster mother fears she has married in a poor one-cow hut.
teaches: Set side by side, the two laments show that imagining the daughter's new home was a set part of the eloped-daughter situation, and that the poets could make it either a blessing or a wound to family pride.

note: Both are the plea of the one left behind against a departure: the couplet says tell your quick return to those still alive; 387 asks him to say he will return, and then shows a road where great men turn back at a lizard's cry.
teaches: The couplet only doubts the traveller's promise; the poem shows why it is empty, since on that road a return depends on omens and beasts, not on the man's word.
audit_text_issue: Lines 4 to 8 and line 20 (சென்றோர் மன்னென இருக்கிற் போர்க்கே) are obscure as printed. | 387 lines 4 to 8 and the last line are syntactically unclear; marker flagged the sense uncertain.

note: Both are the man's account of a first sight, and both set a simple girl (பேதை) against eyes that make war (அமர்த்தன / அமர்த்தனள்).
teaches: The couplet's paradox of war-making eyes in an artless girl gets a cause in the poem: she glares because a stranger blocks her road and jokes about her body, so the 'deadly' look is her self-possession, and it ends in a smile.

note: Both speak of a lover who took a woman's beauty in exchange: the couplet's woman says he took grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor; the courtesan of 396 demands her beauty back before he goes.
teaches: Read together they show the claim that a lover owes back the beauty he took was not the wife's alone: the courtesan states it as a debt to be repaid, which the couplet's wife can only lament.
audit_text_issue: ak396 l.10 மார்புதரு கல்லாய் is uncertain.

note: Both are Paranar's courtesan poems, both end with the demand to give back her beauty and then go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே), and both use the Kaviri carrying off Aththi.
teaches: In 376 the river's seizing of Aththi is left without its tenor; 396 names it (I fear your wife will take you as the Kaviri hid Aththi), so the legend served Paranar as a fixed figure for the wife's lawful claim over the courtesan.

note: 208 tells how Aay Eyinan fell to Minjili at Paazhi and the birds shaded him; 396 says he died because he had promised 'fear not' to those Nannan drove from Punnadu.
teaches: 396 supplies the cause behind 208's famous death: Eyinan died keeping a promise of refuge, which is why a courtesan could cite him against a lover who broke an oath made before a god.

note: Kanaiyan appears in 44 as the chief captured by the Chola after Pazhaiyan fell, and in 386 as the patron shamed when Paanan broke his Aariya wrestler.
teaches: The akam poets used Kanaiyan only in defeat, once in capture and once in public shame, so his name had become a byword for humiliation before an onlooking crowd, which is exactly what the wife of 386 feels.

note: Puram 2 praises the Chera as வான வரம்பன், whose realm runs from the sea of sunrise to the sea of sunset; in 389 the husband goes beyond Vaana varamban's good land into tiger country.
teaches: The title that in puram means a king bounded only by the sky becomes in akam the edge of the safe world: the lover's journey is measured as going past a realm that claims to have no beyond.

note: Both are Mamoolanar's comfort poems: the man has gone beyond Pulli's good land (புல்லி நன்னாட்டு உம்பர்), where herders feed travellers, and he will not delay (நீடலர்).
teaches: Together they show a fixed comforting formula in which the herders' hospitality on Pulli's road is the reason the friend gives for the man's safety, so the same road scene doubles as evidence that he will come back.

note: In 391 the wife sees the tuft he dressed with athiral and mullai and remembers; in 393 the friend says he cannot stay away, having forgotten the sleep beside her hair dressed with blue lily and summer athiral.
teaches: The athiral in her hair is the shared token of the separation: for the wife it is proof of loss, while the friend turns the same token into proof that he must return.

note: Both are hill poems spoken at the night meeting with the lover listening, and both turn on the household's possession rite for Murugan.
teaches: The rite works two ways in the kurinji poems: in 382 its threat is news to hurry the lover, while in 388 the girl plans to use the diviner's own diagnosis to name the hunter, so the rite becomes the channel through which secret love is disclosed.

note: 394 invites the lover to eat milk rice in a mullai village home 'as your wife prepares it'; 384 shows the returned husband bringing a guest into such a home, where the wife receives him.
teaches: The friend's invitation in 394 pictures, as a reason to marry, the very scene 384 shows as marriage achieved: a mullai home where the wife serves guests.

note: Both foster mothers set the girl's flight against a festival at home: in 385 a festival is prepared and the girl says nothing; in 397 the youth will not take her in marriage at the house where the drum never dries.
teaches: Read together they show the elopement grieved as a refused home wedding, blamed in one poem on the girl's silence and in the other on the youth's haste.
audit_text_issue: 397 line 2 and 385 lines 6-7 are uncertain in this text. | Both verses are flagged uncertain; 397 line 2 is hard to construe.

note: Both name the god by his marks, the konrai, the matted hair and the woman who is part of him; Purananuru 1 lists them without a name, Tirumanthiram 16 calls him the one whose part is the bright-browed woman.
teaches: Set beside Tirumular, the anthology's invocation shows that konrai, matted hair and the woman-part were already a fixed set of marks that identified the god without his name, and it adds what Tirumular's verse lacks: the god may also hide that female form within himself.

note: 3 ends by calling the ending of suppliants' poverty the king's true strength (வன்மை); Kural 225 ranks the strength of removing others' hunger above the strength of enduring one's own.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of strengths is abstract, and the Pandya counsel turns it into a test of practice: the giver must read the need from the face before it is spoken, and the deadly road the suppliants crossed measures what that strength owes them.

note: 5 tells the king not to side with those who cast off grace (அருள்) and love and take a hell that never leaves; Kural 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the dark, painful world.
teaches: The Kural makes grace a person's safeguard against hell; the Chera counsel turns the same link into a rule of government, where grace is shown by guarding the realm as one rears a child and hell is the lot of rulers who drop it.

note: Both use the weighing balance for leaning to no side: 6 wishes the king may not hold to one side, like the beam of a balance (தெரிகோல் ஞமன்ன் போல); Kural 118 makes not leaning, like a levelled scale, the ornament of the worthy.
teaches: The same balance serves as a king's blessing in the Purananuru and as a general virtue in the Kural, which shows that impartiality was pictured as a public act of weighing done by whoever judges, before it was a disposition of the private person.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:6 line 9 'ஞமன்ன்' has a doubled final consonant (ஞமன்).

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows; 6 asks the king's umbrella and head to bow before the god's shrine and the sages, his garland to wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands, and his anger to yield before his women's sulking.
teaches: Where the Kural makes humility a constant trait of the great, the Purananuru poet gives it addresses: the king bows to god, sages and wives and to no one on the field, so royal humility was a question of before whom, not of always.

note: 9 praises the Pandya who, before battle, tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter; Kural 773 calls generous help to the foe in misfortune the cutting edge of valour.
teaches: The Kural puts mercy at the end of valour, once the foe has fallen; the Purananuru shows a king putting it before the first arrow by warning those who cannot fight, so the restraint of the brave had a set procedure as well as a maxim.

note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

note: Kural 541 makes justice an inquiry without favour to anyone (கண்ணோடாது); 10 praises a king who lessens the penalty when the offender submits.
teaches: Read together they show that the old ideal allowed mercy after the verdict but not favour within it: the Kural bars kindly regard in the inquiry, while the Purananuru king reduces the sentence for submission, not for kinship or closeness.

note: 11 lists as glory the gold jewels and the silver-strung gold lotus a conquering Chera gave his singer and bard; 12 asks a Pandya whether giving bards gold lotuses and poets chariots is dharma when it comes from land taken to others' pain.
teaches: Side by side, the two poems show that the anthology did not take the gift economy on trust: the gold lotus that crowns the bard in 11 becomes in 12 a question about where a king's gifts come from.

note: 12 asks whether gifts made from others' land, taken so that it pains them, are dharma; Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears.
teaches: Nettimaiyar leaves his question to the king, and the Kural answers it with a law of return, which shows that the poet's courteous irony carries a real moral charge against the plunder that pays for the bards' gifts.

note: 14 praises the king's hands, hardened by goad, bowstring and giving, against the soft hands of his poets, which do nothing but eat; Kural 1035 honours those who eat from their own hands' work, who do not beg and who give to those who ask.
teaches: In the Kural the hand that works for its food is the hand that gives; Kapilar reverses the order and makes the poets' soft, idle hands the proof of the patron's care, so the court valued being fed as a sign of the giver's greatness where the Kural values self-support.

note: Both praise the same Pandya, Mudukudumi: 9 for warning cows, brahmins, women and the sick to shelter before battle; 15 for ploughing enemy towns with donkeys, driving chariots over their fields and bathing his elephants in their guarded tanks.
teaches: The pair shows that the righteous warning of 9 limited whom the king would kill, not what he would destroy: the same king who spares cows and the sick ploughs the enemy city into waste.

note: 16 praises a Chola for turning cool sugarcane fields into waste and feeding fire to a safe land; 18 tells a Pandya that food is land joined with water and that those who give food give life.
teaches: The anthology holds both the vanji boast of burned farmland and the counsel that farmland is life, which shows that the counsel of 18 was a duty owed to one's own land, while the enemy's fields remained a fit measure of glory.

note: 17 praises the Irumporai as lord of cool Thondi, with screwpine, wide fields, sandy groves and backwaters; Akananuru 60 compares a fisherman's guarded daughter's beauty to Thondi of the Porayan of the strong chariots.
teaches: The Poraiyan port that the praise poet counts among the king's possessions became, in akam, the standard for a girl's well-guarded beauty, which shows love poets taking their measure of value from the Chera wealth that puram poets praised.

note: Kural 542 says the whole world lives looking to the sky and the people to the ruler's sceptre; 18 says land that sows and looks to the sky (வித்திவான் நோக்கும் புன்புலம்) does not help its ruler however wide, and tells him to build tanks.
teaches: Where the Kural sets rain and the sceptre side by side as the two things people depend on, Kudapulaviyanar makes the ruler answerable for freeing the land from the sky, turning dependence on rain into a duty of public works.

note: 18 opens its argument with bodies that cannot exist without water (நீர்இன்று அமையா யாக்கை); Kural 20 says the world cannot go on without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு).
teaches: The two share the phrase but draw different conclusions from it: the Kural derives the world's dependence on the sky, the Purananuru the king's duty to store water, so one premise supported both a praise of rain and a policy against relying on it.

note: Both name Nedunchezhiyan's victory over the seven at Alankanam (ஆலங் கானத்து; எழுவர் நல்வலம்): 19 shows the field where mothers wept and Death fled ashamed, Akananuru 36 makes the victors' shout there the measure of how loud the gossip about the hero is.
teaches: The akam poet borrowed only the victors' roar from Alankanam to measure a scandal, while the puram poem on the same battle keeps the weeping of the old houses' women, so one battle served love poetry as a byword for noise and praise poetry as a field of grief.

note: 20 ends: all living beings fear (அஞ்சும்) you; Kural 563 says a ruler who acts so as to cause dread perishes quickly. On the reading that the beings fear the king, 20 praises what the Kural condemns; on the reading that they fear for him, the two agree.
teaches: The ambiguity of 20's last line matters because the Kural's chapter against causing dread makes a feared king a doomed king, so Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar's praise only holds if the people's fear is anxiety for their ruler and not dread of him.

note: Kural 743 defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; 21 describes Kanapper with a moat beyond depth, a sky-high wall and a sunless guard forest, and praises the king who took it.
teaches: The puram poet uses the full list of what makes a fort good only to measure the man who took it, so the Kural's criteria guarantee nothing to the defender: in the praise poem a perfect fort is the conqueror's ornament.

note: Both by Kalladanar to Nedunchezhiyan: 23 ends on a doe and fawn whose stag the tiger has killed; 25 ends on widows beating their breasts and shearing their hair.
teaches: The same poet states openly in 25 what 23 leaves as a bare image, which supports reading the bereaved doe of 23 as the enemy's widows and shows that a puram poet could move between the hidden and the stated forms of one grief.

note: 23 praises the victor of Alankanam; Akananuru 175 compares the lightning of the returning rains to the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alankanam.
teaches: The heroine's speech in an akam poem borrows the Pandya's Alankanam victory, which 23 celebrates as fact, to measure the flashing of the rains that mark her lover's promised return, so a war became a stock image of brilliance within the poets' own generation.

note: 24 names the Mizhalai of Evvi, the generous Vel, among the lands Chezhiyan holds; Akananuru 266 names Evvi of Needur, true of sword, and the uproar after his men's victory.
teaches: One chief is remembered in the Purananuru for open-handed giving and for lands that passed to the Pandya, and in the Akananuru as a byword for the din of his war victory, so the akam poets kept a lesser king's martial name alive as a measure of loud gossip.

note: 24 ends: those who knew say the ones who truly lived are those who did not go as the many go but stood and died with lasting fame; Kural 240 says those who live without renown do not live.
teaches: The Kural's flat verdict appears in 24 as a saying the poet attributes to the wise and sets after a blessing of royal pleasure, so the maxim was already proverbial and served to bend a feast poem toward the thought of death.

note: 26 calls Chezhiyan அடுகளம் வேட்ட, the one who sacrificed the killing field; Akananuru 36 measures the town's gossip by the roar when Chezhiyan at Alankanam களம்வேட்ட, after killing seven kings in one day.
teaches: The same phrase for the battlefield sacrifice appears in a praise poem and in a heroine's quarrel with her husband, which shows the Pandya's war rite was famous enough as a phrase to serve an akam speaker as the loudest noise she could name.

note: 27 line 6 மரைஇலை போல மாய்ந்திசினோர் பலரே (many died like the lotus leaf); Naladiyar 359 ends மரையிலையின் மாய்ந்தார் பலர் (many perished like the lotus leaf).
teaches: The Naladiyar repeats the Purananuru's half-line almost word for word but moves it from nobly born kings who died without a poet's praise to people whose expectations came to nothing, and the earlier poem shows what the lotus-leaf death meant: dying without a name, beside the flower that is remembered.

note: 27 reports the saying that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car that no charioteer drives; Kural 234 says that if one wins long fame on earth, the gods' world does not honour the புலவர்.
teaches: The belief that poets' praise carries a man to heaven, which 27 gives as current hearsay, is the background the elliptical couplet assumes when it ties earthly fame to the gods' world, so the Purananuru supplies the premise the Kural leaves out.
audit_text_issue: Kural 234 sense uncertain (marker's flag).

note: 28 tells the king his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failure would be his own neglect; Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means without wrong yields virtue and pleasure.
teaches: The Kural makes the yield of virtue and pleasure depend on how wealth was gained, while the court poet makes it depend on whether the king takes care to use it, so the two books place the moral test of wealth at opposite ends, getting and spending.

note: 29 sets its blessing in a world where people pass in turn like players at a festival; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd that gathers at a dance hall and disperses.
teaches: Both books reach for the festival stage to show transience, but the Purananuru applies it to the players, the people themselves, and draws the counsel to turn stored wealth into fame, while the Kural applies it to the audience, wealth itself, so the same image grounds two different lessons about what passes.
audit_text_issue: 29 is flagged uncertain; line 2 ஐது அடர்ந்ற looks misprinted.

note: 31 opens: as wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, so the two other kings' umbrellas follow behind Nalankilli's; Kural 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy.
teaches: The ordering the Kural states as an ethical rule is used by the court poet as a ready image to rank three crowned kings, which shows the precedence of virtue over wealth and pleasure was a commonplace secure enough to carry a political claim.

note: 34 quotes dharma: there is expiation for killing cows' udders, destroying unborn children or wronging elders, but none for killing a benefit; Kural 110 says those who killed any good may escape, but not one who killed a good done to him.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a rule what the Purananuru presents as a known saying with its list of lesser crimes, and the poet turns it on himself, so the maxim was already used to bind a bard to praise his patron: gratitude here is the poet's own obligation, not only the patron's claim.

note: 35 says the king's umbrella is for sheltering his people and his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; Kural 1034 says those with the shade of grain-ears see many kings' umbrellas under their own king's umbrella.
teaches: Both texts set the royal umbrella against the farmer and make conquest depend on the plough, but 35 says it to the king as counsel while the Kural says it of the farmer as praise, so the same economic claim is spoken from both ends of the realm.

note: 35 says rain comes when sought in the land of the just sceptre, but also that the world blames kings for failed rains and harvests; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules rightly.
teaches: The Kural states the link between just rule and rain as a fact, while the court poet adds that people will blame the king for drought whatever its cause, so in the Purananuru the doctrine is also a political danger the king must manage.
audit_text_issue: Line 15 முறைவெண்டு is likely முறைவேண்டு; line 17 கொண்டுமூ is likely கொண்மூ.

note: 36 tells the besieging king that to have fought a rival who sits at ease behind his walls is a matter of shame; Naladiyar 241 says the worthy, seeing their enemies humbled, feel shame and do not advance.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim about shame before a humbled foe is in 36 an actual plea to stop a siege, which shows the poets used this sense of honour to bring wars to an end, and that the shame was felt to fall on the victor.

note: Both by Nappasalaiyar to Killivalavan open by naming him the descendant of the Chola who relieved a dove's distress (37 புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த; 39 the king who entered the scale for the dove).
teaches: The poet uses one ancestral legend of mercy in opposite ways: in 37 it heads praise of a king who spares no fine town, and in 39 it is set aside as inherited fame that cannot be his own, so the legend served both to honour the line and to ask what the living king had added.

note: 38 says heaven lacks giving and asking, so gift-seekers prefer the king's land; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: Both books cut the worth of giving loose from heaven, but from opposite sides: the Kural says giving is good even without a heaven to reward it, and the Purananuru says heaven is poorer than earth because no one gives there, so giving becomes what makes this world worth more than the next.

note: 40 asks the conqueror to be sweet of speech and easy of access (இன்சொல் எண்பதத்தை); Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others.
teaches: The Kural's two marks of a praised king are in 40 exactly the two requests a poet puts to a victorious king, so the couplet's criteria were the counsel bards gave in person, and the poem ties them to the king's fame among his poets.

note: 41 opens 'காலனும் காலம் பார்க்கும்' (even Death watches for its time) to say the king does not wait; Naladiyar 36 tells the reader not to ask whether Death comes today or another day, for it stands right behind.
teaches: Both treat Death as an agent that chooses its hour, but the Purananuru makes that patience the measure a king exceeds, while the Naladiyar makes the unknown hour the reason for doing good now, so one belief about death supports a war boast in one book and a moral urgency in the other.

note: Kural 544: the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people and rules by the sceptre; 42: under his unbending sceptre the land knows no war cry, and all poets turn to him as rivers run to the sea.
teaches: The Kural states the reciprocity abstractly, while 42 shows what the embrace consists of (fields that feed guests, no raid-cry heard) and what the turning to the king looks like (poets flowing in like rivers), so the couplet's 'world at his feet' can be read as a picture of a watered, hospitable country.

note: Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for another's fault as for their own the dwelling place of shame; in 43 the prince, wronged by the poet's words, is ashamed 'as if you had erred' (நீபிழைத் தாய்போல் நனிநா ணினையே).
teaches: The Kural's definition of the finest shame is acted out in 43 by a prince who blushes for the man who insulted him, and the poem adds the consequence the couplet omits: that shame shown this way disarms the offender, who then takes the fault on himself.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

note: 45 warns two Cholas that their quarrel will give deep delight to other kings; Akananuru 346 closes on a Chola, Killi Valavan, worsted at Koodal and 'Kothai Marban's joy was great'.
teaches: An akam poet's closing allusion records exactly the outcome Kovur Kizhar predicted in puram, a rival Chera rejoicing at a Chola defeat, which shows that akam poets drew on the same remembered politics of the three crowns (whether this Killi Valavan is 45's Chola is not certain).

note: Both poems address Chola princes as descendants of the king who saved the dove (புறவு): 43 to rebuke a prince, 46 to stop the killing of children.
teaches: Placed together, the two poems show the dove story working as a family standard that poets could hold up to any Chola, in 43 to shame and in 46 to restrain, so the legend served as a check on royal conduct, not only as praise.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: 48 praises Thondi of the seaside grove, the Chera's town, as fragrant with the king's garland and the neytal of its backwater; Akananuru 60 likens the heroine's bright bangles to Thondi of Poraiyan of the strong chariot.
teaches: The same Chera port that a puram poet offers as his home and his king's glory becomes in an akam poem a measure of a girl's beauty, which shows that akam poets used a king's famous town as a byword for desirable wealth.

note: 49 asks how to name Kothai of the raised sword; Akananuru 346 ends on Kothai Marban rejoicing when a Chola was worsted at Koodal.
teaches: The Chera whom a puram poet praises as lord of three landscapes appears in akam as a rival who delights in a Chola defeat, which shows akam poets citing a living king's partisanship, not only his wealth, and lets the reader see the three-crown politics behind the praise (whether both name the same Kothai is not certain).

note: 50 says the king spared and fanned the poet as if he had heard that the higher world has a dwelling only for those with fame here; Kural 234 says that if one wins wide fame on earth the world of the gods does not honour the learned (or the gods) instead.
teaches: Both tie fame on earth to standing in the world beyond, and 50 shows the belief at work in a single act of royal mercy, while the Kural states it as a rule whose terms are disputed; the poem suggests that for a Sangam king fame was a practical reason for forbearance.

note: 51 and 52 are both poems to Maran Vazhuthi: 51 says the kings who resisted him are pitiable, living a day like winged termites; 52 shows what that pity means, their towns turning to jungle and their common hall abandoned.
teaches: Read in sequence, 51 gives the general verdict and 52 the landscape of its execution, so the reader sees how Sangam praise of a conqueror moved from a simile of brief life to a detailed picture of a deserted village.

note: Kural 1055: askers can stand before people because there are those on earth who do not hide what they have; 54: suppliants walk into the king's court 'as if they owned it' (உடையோர் போல), because he gives without stint.
teaches: The Kural explains why asking is possible at all, and 54 shows the confidence such a giver creates, a beggar entering a court with raised head; the poem also adds the other face the Kural omits, the same king's land as a tiger's ground to his rivals.

note: 55: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors are excellent, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; Kural 546: it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: The Purananuru poet already ranks the four-limbed army below righteous rule before the Kural's couplet does, and he spells out the straight sceptre as impartiality toward one's own and others, so the Kural's maxim had a court-counsel form addressed to a named Pandya.
audit_text_issue: Line count differs from one edition (23 vs 21 lines); line 14 has stray punctuation.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting after inquiry without favour to anyone; 55 asks the king not to bend the rod because a man is 'ours' and not to destroy merit because he is 'others'.
teaches: The Kural forbids favour in one direction only, while 55 names both failures, favouring one's own and injuring outsiders, so the poem shows that impartiality was understood as a double duty, protecting strangers' merit as well as resisting kin.

note: 55 asks the king to be like the sun in fierce valour and like the moon in cool gentleness; 59 says the king is like the sun to his enemies and the moon to people like the poet.
teaches: The same sun-and-moon pair is counsel in 55 and description in 59, so the anthology shows a stock image of kingship moving between what a king should be and what a poet says he already is, with the second poem naming whom each face is turned to.

note: 56 names the palmyra-bannered god and the sapphire-dark god among the four guardians of the world; 58 likens the allied Chola and Pandya to the two great gods, the milk-white one with the palmyra banner and the blue one with the wheel, standing together.
teaches: One poem divides the two gods among four to praise one king, the other pairs them to praise two allied kings, so the reader sees that poets chose a god-pair or a god-set to match the number and relation of the kings they praised.

note: 52 dwells on the enemy's land turned to jungle as the measure of the king's glory; 57 permits plunder, burning and killing in the enemy's land but asks the king to spare the guardian trees.
teaches: Set beside 52's relish of devastation, 57 shows that the same war poetry also drew a limit, and drew it at the sacred tree rather than at people, which tells us what the poets held more inviolable than the lives of the conquered.

note: 58 warns two allied kings against outsiders who come between them 'seeming good, seeming kind, seeming to follow the old ways'; Kural 826 says the words of the unreconciled, though they speak good things like friends, are soon seen through.
teaches: The Kural's general warning about feigned friendship is applied in 58 to an alliance of kings, where the danger is not the enemy's attack but his pleasant counsel, so the pair shows the couplet's subject was already a matter of statecraft.
audit_text_issue: 58 lines 6 and 7 (கிளைஅரா எறியும், அருநரை உருமின்) are obscure, as the marker notes.

note: 45 tells two quarrelling Cholas that their fight will delight other kings; 58 tells a Chola and a Pandya that if they never break their union the whole earth will be theirs.
teaches: The two poems state one calculation from opposite sides, division gives the gain to outsiders and union takes it from them, so together they show Sangam poets thinking of alliances between crowns in terms of who profits.

note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

note: Akananuru 55's mother, sleepless after her daughter's elopement, compares her lot to the noble men who, hearing Cheralathan's bitter words when he sat north after Venni, went with him to the other world; 65 laments the same king's sitting north (வடக்கு இருந்தனன்) out of shame at a back wound.
teaches: The akam poet can use the king's death as a simile for a mother's loss only because puram poems such as 65 had made it known, and the akam poem adds what 65 does not say: that men of his court followed him into death, so the two together give the event and its aftermath.

note: Both poems are on the death after Venni: 65 mourns the king who sat north ashamed of a back wound, and 66, addressed to the victor Karikal, says that king is better than him; both use the phrase புறப்புண் நாணி.
teaches: Read together they show the honour code reversing a battle's result: the loser's chosen death, mourned in 65 as the stopping of a whole country's life, is used in 66 to rank him above the victor, said to the victor's face.

note: Akananuru 246's friend says the gossip about the hero was louder than the uproar at Venni when Karikal broke the strength of kings and eleven Velir and their drums were left on the field.
teaches: The akam poet remembers Venni for the noise of Karikal's victory over many kings, while 66 remembers it for the defeated king's honourable death, so one battle served akam as a measure of loudness and puram as a lesson in honour.

note: Kural 970 says the world praises the radiance of those who will not live when disgrace comes; 66 says the king who sat north ashamed of his wound reached the world of great fame (மிகப் புகழ் உலகம்).
teaches: 66 shows what the Kural's general praise of honour could mean in practice: a dishonour as small as a wound's place on the body, a death chosen for it, and a poet ranking the dead man above the living victor in public.

note: The half-line எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க (the strength of the seven brought down) stands in 76 line 12 and in Akananuru 36 line 20, both of Cheliyan's victory at Alankanam; Akananuru 36 names the seven kings.
teaches: The identical half-line shows that the Alankanam victory had a fixed formula that passed from praise poetry into akam, where the war-cry of that day becomes the measure of how loud the town's gossip is about the hero's new bride.

note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

note: In 72 the king accepts, if he breaks his vow, that his people will find no shade under his rule and will weep and blame him as cruel; Kural 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering are what wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: The Kural names the people's tears as a force that destroys a king's wealth; 72 shows a king himself choosing those tears as the worst penalty he could stake, so the Kural's warning was already a ruler's own measure of failure.

note: In 72 the kings mock Neduncheliyan as a boy (இளையன் இவன்); in 78 the new warriors say 'the fighter is young' (பொருநனும் இளையன்) and are pursued to their fathers' town and killed.
teaches: 78 tells, through a court poet, the sequel that 72 vows in the king's own voice, so the anthology keeps both the vow and its fulfilment, and the taunt of youth becomes the hinge of the king's fame.

note: 77 pictures the king as a boy just weaned, with the child's amulet still on; 72 is the same king's vow against kings who mocked him as young.
teaches: 77 shows that the enemies' taunt in 72 was literally true, which makes the boy's vow and its performance the more striking and explains why his poets kept returning to his age.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:72 line 1 'நகுதத் கனரே' is corrupt (நகுதக் கனரே).

note: Among the curses 71 accepts is to put an incapable man in office in his assembly out of fondness (அன்பின் அவையத்துத் திறன்இல் ஒருவனை நாட்டி); Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every kind of folly.
teaches: The Kural names fondness as the cause of a bad appointment; 71 shows how grave such an appointment was held to be, since a king lists it among the curses on himself beside losing his wife, his friends and his birthright.

note: 73 says the fool who ignored the strength of the strong (ஆற்றல் உடையோர் ஆற்றல் போற்றாது) will hardly escape alive; Kural 891 says not slighting the strength of those able to act (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை) is the chief of all safeguards.
teaches: The near-identical wording shows the Kural turning a king's threat into a general safeguard: what 73 says from the side of the strong man about to strike, the Kural says to everyone who might provoke him.

note: 74 asks whether a warrior line would bear a son who begs a little drink to quench his hunger; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow degrades the tongue more than anything.
teaches: The Kural makes asking shameful even for the worthiest cause; 74 roots the same horror in a warrior code that will not let even a stillborn child go unmarked by the sword, so the shame of begging is shown as a matter of lineage as well as of general ethics.

note: 75's petty heir begs dues from his people (குடிபுரவு இரக்கும்); Kural 552 says the asking (இரவு) of a king with his sceptre is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over'.
teaches: Both books call a king's demand on his people begging, and 75 adds the cause the Kural leaves out: the petty heir values the throne as wealth to take from, where the worthy one counts the same fortune as light as a dry stick.

note: In 67 Pisir Aandhai trusts that King Killi will reward a swan for saying it serves at his feet; in 216 Kopperuncholan tells his doubting courtiers that the poet, whom he knows only by hearing, will come.
teaches: Each partner stakes something on the other's regard for a name alone: the poet promises the king's gift for it, the king promises the poet's arrival, so the anthology keeps this friendship from both sides.

note: 68 promises the bard a lord who will give so much that he forgets other men's doors (பிறன்கடை மறப்ப); Kural 1053 says even asking has a grace when one stands before those who hide nothing and know their duty.
teaches: The Kural allows asking only before the right giver, and the guide poem is the bard's practical answer: it tells him which door to stand at so that he need never stand at another, which shows ஆற்றுப்படை solving the Kural's problem of asking.

note: 70 says the king's giving is no windfall like woodcutters finding gold; Kural 216 likens the wealth of the good-hearted man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: 70 makes explicit what the Kural's tree in the town only implies: the value of a generous man's wealth to those who ask is that it can be counted on, unlike a lucky find, so reliability is part of what giving means.

note: Both poems, by Kazhathalaiyar and Paranar, are on the battle in which Neduncheralathan and Peruvirarkilli both died; both list the fallen army and silent drums and both kings dead.
teaches: Two poets on the same double death close differently, one with heaven's feast and a blessing on fame, the other with a question about the orphaned land, so the thokai nilai could console with glory or count the cost to the country.

note: Akananuru 6 calls Tittan of Uranthai the great giver who brings the wealth of rain (மாவண் தித்தன்); 80 asks Tittan to witness the hero's victory 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Tittan's fame as a giver as a byword, while 80 makes his grace toward one man uncertain, so the same chief appears as a public giver and as a withholding judge whose favour must be won.

note: 84 says her lord has great shoulders though he eats புற்கை (coarse gruel); Kural 1065 says that even gruel thin as water (அடுபுற்கை) is sweetest when one's own effort earned it.
teaches: The Kural's gruel of the self-reliant poor already stood in the older poem for a strong man's austere fare, cited by a woman as proof of his strength, so the couplet's dignity of plain food draws on a heroic image, not only on poverty.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:84 line 1 என்ஜ is corrupt (for என்னை)

note: 85 describes a crowd split into two sides over the contest, one saying he wins and one saying he does not; 83 curses 'this bewildered town, split two ways and never on one side' (இருபாற் பட்ட).
teaches: Read with 85, the divided town of 83 is a crowd taking sides over Killi's contest, so the woman's curse wishes her own inner division onto spectators who argue about the very man she loves.

note: Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him; in 86 a mother likens her womb to a tiger's empty den and says her son will be found on the battlefield.
teaches: The Kural's mother waits to hear others praise her son, while the Purananuru mother does not know where he is and stakes her pride on her womb and the battlefield, which shows that the worth a mother hoped for could be a warrior's death as readily as a good name.

note: 86's mother says her son will show himself on the battlefield; in 278 an old mother searches the battlefield and rejoices more than at his birth on finding her son fallen with his body cut apart.
teaches: Together the two run from boast to proof: the field where 86's son will 'appear' is the field 278's mother has to search among the corpses, and the joy she measures against the day of birth is the price of the first mother's confidence.

note: 87 opens களம்புகல் ஓம்புமின், தெவ்விர் (enemies, beware of entering the field); Kural 771 opens என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் (enemies, do not stand before my lord).
teaches: The Kural's chapter on an army's pride keeps a whole Sangam speech-type, the warning to foes addressed as தெவ்விர் with a prohibitive verb, and swaps Avvai's craftsman's image of strength for the hero-stones of the slain, so the couplet is the genre cut down to its threat.

note: Both are Avvai's warnings to Anji's foes under the thurai தானை மறம், each built on the imperative ஓம்புமின் (beware).
teaches: Side by side they show the formula's moving part: 87 rests the threat on one unnamed warrior wrought like a month-made wheel, 88 on the chief himself in his finery, so the same prohibition could be backed by the army or by the king.

note: 90 asks whether deer herds can stand where a fierce tiger rages; Kural 599 says even a huge, sharp-tusked elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
teaches: In both the tiger is the spirit that neither numbers nor size can resist, but Avvai sets it on a herd to praise a king while the Kural sets it on an elephant to teach ookkam, so one image served both royal praise and a general maxim on energy.
audit_text_issue: kural:599 line 2 has a corrupted letter (஦வ்ருஉம் for வெரூஉம்)

note: Kural 82: even if it were the medicine of deathlessness, eating it alone while the guest waits outside is not to be wished; in 91 Anji gives Avvai the nelli fruit that keeps death away instead of eating it.
teaches: The Kural's extreme case, the food of immortality not eaten alone, has a remembered instance in a chieftain who gave a poet the fruit of long life, so the maxim's hyperbole was also a story the tradition told of a real giver.

note: 91 thanks Anji for giving Avvai the nelli fruit so that she might escape death; 235, Avvai's lament for him, recalls how he shared toddy and food with her and says the spear that pierced him fell on the tongues of poets.
teaches: The gift of long life in 91 turns bitter in 235: the poet made to outlive her patron is left to mourn him, and the spear that killed the giver silences the singers he fed, so the pair binds the bard's fortune to the patron's life.

note: 91 calls Anji lord of the Athiyar with கழல்தொடி தடக்கை; Akananuru 162 names a கழல்தொடி அதிகன் who never fails the hope of suppliants and owns a hill of jackfruit and vengai (probably the same Athiyar house, though the akam poem does not say which chief).
teaches: An akam poet uses the same epithet and the same fame for never failing those who ask, which 91 shows in one deed, to set the hill where a lover recalls a hard-won meeting, so the Athiyar chief's giving was a byword love poets could lean on.

note: 92: a child's prattle does not keep to the lute and makes no sense, yet moves fathers; Kural 66: those who call the flute and lute sweet have not heard their children's prattle.
teaches: The Kural leaves unsaid that prattle fails every test of music, and Avvai says it outright and builds on it, so read together the father's delight is shown to be grace rather than taste, which is what lets her use it for a patron's love of an imperfect poem.

note: Kural 776: the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound (விழுப்புண்); 93 tells how a king who died of sickness was cut with a sword on darbha grass so as to go where the battle-slain go, and ends on Anji's விழுப்புண்.
teaches: The poem shows why a day without a wound could be counted lost: a death without one had to be given a wound by rite before the dead could reach the heroes' world, so the Kural's ledger rests on a belief about where the dead go.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:93 lines 2-11 are compressed in syntax.

note: 94: gentle to us like the bull elephant that lets village boys wash its tusks, harsh to foes like its musth; 315: Anji can stay unseen like the fire-stick tucked in the eaves and blaze like the fire it kindles.
teaches: Avvai gives Anji the same two-sided nature twice in different images, gentle and fierce in 94, hidden and blazing in 315, which shows that the double character, not any single image, was her settled portrait of him.

note: 95: he gives food when he has it and eats together with the poor when he has none; 315: when he has, he can eat, and he gives to suppliants even beyond what he owes.
teaches: Both poems answer the same question, what Anji does when his stores run low, and together show that his fame as a giver rests on sharing want with his dependants, not on abundance.

note: Kural 227: the disease called hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; 95 praises a lord who shares when he has and goes without together with his dependants when he has not.
teaches: The Kural promises the habitual sharer freedom from hunger, while Avvai's lord shares and still has empty days, so the poem shows the virtue the Kural rewards at work in a world where sharing did not prevent want but made it common to all.

note: 97 lists Anji's swords, spears, elephants and horses worn by war and tells enemies to pay tribute; 98 lists what his enemies do on seeing his elephants, horses, spear and warriors, and ends in pity for their doomed land.
teaches: The two catalogues show one army from two sides, its weapons worn out in 97 and the enemy's barred gates and bound wounds in 98, so the tribute demanded in 97 is backed by the ruin of fields that 98 foresees.

note: 99 says Anji is beyond ordinary singers and that Paranar sang his victory at Kovalur; in Akananuru 352 the heroine calls her friend's news sweeter than a bard's famous song that set Anji's renown.
teaches: The akam heroine's comparison assumes that songs fixing Anji's fame were well known and loved, which 99 confirms by naming a poet who sang it, so a puram repertoire stands behind the love poem's simile.

note: 100 ends with the eyes that glared at foes staying red even when he looks at his small son; Kural 775 calls it defeat if the glaring eye blinks when a spear is thrown.
teaches: The Kural asks the warrior's glare not to waver before a spear, and Avvai shows it cannot waver even before his own child, so together the fixed red eye is both the warrior's ideal and a cost the poem lets the reader feel.

note: Both Avvai on Athiyaman (101) and Kapilar on Pari (114) use the elephant's food-ball (கவளம்) as their simile: held safe between the tusks in 101, chewed and dropped in 114.
teaches: The same image of a patron's court serves praise and lament: in the living patron's poem the food-ball is the gift kept safe for the bard, and in the dead patron's poem it is the dropped leavings that mark where feasts used to be.

note: 101 argues at length that Athiyaman's gift never fails however long it is delayed; the akam poem 162 calls Athikan, of the same house, one who never let a suppliant's hope fail (நசைபிழைப்பு அறியா).
teaches: What 101 has to argue as a bard's private reassurance had become, in an akam poet's line, a fixed epithet of the Athiyaman house, so the praise poem shows the experience behind the epithet.

note: 102 likens the prince to the spare axle salt-carters (உமணர்) tie under a loaded cart; in 116 Pari's orphaned daughters climb a heap of leaves to count the salt-carters' carts going by.
teaches: The salt caravan stands for dependence on a protector in praise and for the loss of one in lament: in 102 the patron is the carters' reserve, in 116 his daughters have nothing to do but watch the carts that no longer concern them.
audit_text_issue: 116 lacks a line after line 9 found in another edition, as the marker notes.

note: 103 is Avvai's guide poem sending a viraliyar to Anji; Akananuru 352 cites a bard's song that set down Anji's good fame (அஞ்சி நல்லிசை நிறுத்த) as a model of fine craft.
teaches: Read together they show the life of a praise song: Avvai directs performers to Anji, and a later akam poet can take a bard's song of Anji's fame as the standard of a well-made song, so the guide poems made the fame the akam poets borrowed.

note: Kural 495 says the crocodile wins in deep water and is killed by anything once out of it; 104 makes the young king a crocodile that kills an elephant in a foot-deep children's pool.
teaches: The Kural uses the crocodile to teach that strength belongs to the ground, while Avvai uses it to claim a strength that needs almost no ground, so a court poet's praise could deny the very limit the ethics book counsels kings to respect.

note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to slight him as young (இளையர்); 104 warns the enemy's warriors not to slight Avvai's lord as young (இளையன்).
teaches: The warning against scorning a young king is a rule of court conduct in the Kural and a battlefield threat in Avvai, which shows the same caution was voiced to subjects as duty and to enemies as danger.

note: Kural 221 calls giving only what goes to those who have nothing, all else being a measured exchange; 106 says Pari holds himself bound to give even to the foolish and the weak, as the gods accept even the erukkam flower.
teaches: The Kural defines true giving by the asker having nothing to return, and Kapilar supplies the image for it, the god who accepts a worthless flower, so the giver's duty is modelled on a god's acceptance rather than on a bargain.

note: Kural 211 says obligation seeks no return, for the world gives nothing back to the rain; 107 says Pari is not the only one, for the rain too sustains the world.
teaches: Kapilar's mock rebuke works only because the comparison of the giver with the rain was already accepted, as the Kural makes it a principle, so the joke assumes the doctrine and the doctrine has here a named man as its model.

note: Naladiyar 97 sets the rain and the world's doing what it should side by side as the two things the world survives by; 107 sets Pari and the rain side by side as sustainers of the world.
teaches: The Naladiyar's pairing of rain with human giving is the background against which 107's line reads as praise, and 107 shows that pairing applied to one patron centuries before it was stated as a general rule.

note: Kural 223 praises giving without uttering the misery of 'I have nothing'; 108 says Pari would not say 'I will not come' even if suppliants asked for him.
teaches: The Kural forbids the giver one refusal, the plea of having nothing; 108 imagines the case past it, where nothing is left and the giver offers himself, so the poem tests the maxim at its limit.

note: 105 sends a viraliyar to Pari with the promise of jewels; 109 tells the besieging kings that the only way to take Parambu is to come as bards with their viralis behind them.
teaches: Kapilar turns his own guide-poem formula into siege terms: the road that brings a performer gifts is the only road into the fort, which shows the guide poem's convention used as a political weapon.

note: 109 says Parambu needs no ploughing because its hill yields four foods by itself; Akananuru 303 describes flocks of sparrows of Pari's Parambu flying out at dawn to bring back red paddy and returning at evening.
teaches: Both describe food coming into Parambu without its people farming, which suggests the self-feeding hill was a known part of Pari's legend that an akam poet could use as a ready simile for something sure to return.

note: 110 tells the three kings that Parambu is hard to take though they join forces; Akananuru 78 recalls Pari, with Kapilar beside him, driving off the tusked kings after years of fighting.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled history what 110 states as a boast during the siege, so the pair shows the defence of Parambu passing from Kapilar's own war-speech into the shared stock of akam similes.

note: 111 says the hill cannot be won by kings with the spear and only a singer can have it; 112 says kings with victorious drums have taken our hill.
teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the boast that the hill could not be taken and the daughters' report that it was taken show how the editors let the poems record the siege's outcome against Kapilar's claim.

note: Naladiyar 3 says even kings who led armies under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and their enemies take their wives; 112 has a giver's daughters say the kings took their hill and they have no father.
teaches: The Naladiyar explains a ruler's fall by his own spent deeds, but 112 gives no cause and its subject is a famous giver, so the lament qualifies the moral account: here loss falls on the blameless and the poem does not explain it.

note: 113 ends with Kapilar leaving Parambu to find husbands for Pari's daughters; in 200 he offers them in marriage to Vichikko.
teaches: The two poems give the beginning and a later stage of one errand: the lament's last line becomes a formal offer in 200, which shows the duty of the dead patron's poet carried out as a sequence of poems.

note: 109 predicts that the besieging kings will not take Parambu by force; 116 recalls that the daughters once counted from the hill the horses of kings who came to fight without knowing Pari's strength, and now count salt carts.
teaches: Read after 109, 116 shows what the confident siege-speech left out: the kings did come, and the poet who promised the fort was safe now measures its fall by what the daughters count.
audit_text_issue: the marker notes a line missing after line 9 and an ambiguous line 14 (வியன்மலை அற்றே)

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a ruler who wields the sceptre rightly; 117 says Pari's land never lacked rain, even under the omens of drought, because of the straightness of his sceptre.
teaches: The Kural's rule is given to crowned kings, and 117 grants it to a hill chief and sets it above the stars' omens, so the poem shows the doctrine of the just sceptre extended to any lord who rules well.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of a kindly man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 119 likens Pari to a lone tree on a long road without shade.
teaches: The Kural puts its tree where everyone can reach it, while 119 puts it where nothing else gives shelter, so the poem adds that a giver's worth is measured by how few others give.

note: Both lists of the land's harvest break off with the same question, நந்துங் கொல்லோ (will it last?), before naming the land as the dead patron's.
teaches: The shared refrain shows the poems were made as a set in which each catalogue of plenty is undercut by the same doubt, so the anthology's sequence on Pari works like a song with a refrain.

note: 121 tells Kari to give up the common gaze (பொது நோக்கு) and know each bard's rank (வரிசை); Kural 528 says a king who looks by rank (வரிசையா) rather than in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) draws many to live around him.
teaches: The Kural's two technical words for graded favour already stand in Kapilar's advice to a patron, so the Kural's rule for a king's kin was first argued by poets about how gifts should be ranked among themselves.

note: 121 says giving is easy and knowing due rank (வரிசை அறிதல்) is hard; 140 shows the lord of Nanjil, 'knowing rank' (வரிசை அறிதலின்), answering a request for rice with an elephant.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show that வரிசை cut both ways: 121 wants the patron to rank the recipient, 140 praises a patron who ranked by his own greatness and so overpaid, so the measure of a gift could be the giver's standing as well as the receiver's worth.

note: 121 asks the patron to stop treating all poets alike; Akananuru 152 praises Ay for giving freely to those who come whether skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும் சென்றோர்க்கு). On the plain reading the two ideals of giving are incompatible.
teaches: The akam poet borrows as an ornament exactly the indiscriminate giving that Kapilar argues against, so the ideal of the patron who gives to all was common fame, and 121 is a poet's dissent from it, not the standard view.

note: 123 praises Malayan of unfading fame (தொலையா நல்லிசை) at Mullur; Akananuru 209 names the Mullur king Kari whose fame does not pass (செல்லா நல்லிசை), who killed Ori and gave the Kolli hills to the Cheras.
