teaches: The akam friend uses Kari's lasting fame as a fixed point to measure the heroine's beauty, which shows that the bards' praise of Kari had become a shared reference that akam poets could cite to measure something else entirely.

note: 126 calls Malaiyaman Kari lord of a land of palmyra groves (பெண்ணையம் படப்பை நாடு); Akananuru 35 names Kari of the long chariot, lord of Kovalur, and the great river Pennai (பெண்ணையம் பேரியாறு) at his ford.
teaches: The mother's lament in Akananuru 35 places her daughter's flight on the river of Kari's land, so a puram patron's territory supplies the akam poem's geography, and the shared பெண்ணையம் suggests that 126's phrase may name the river land rather than palms alone.

note: 128 says Ay's Pothiyil may be approached only by a dancing woman, while proud kings can hardly come near; Akananuru 322 compares the beloved, hard to win, to Pothiyil, hard to enter (புகலரும் பொதியில் போல).
teaches: The akam lover's simile takes its force from the puram boast: Pothiyil's inaccessibility was a known fact of Ay's power, and the akam poet turned a chief's closed hill into a measure of a woman's reserve.

note: 122 says nothing is Kari's own except his wife (நினது என இலை); 135 wishes Ay long life with the inheritance he does not grasp as his (எமதெனப் பற்றல் தேற்றா).
teaches: Two poets praising two different chiefs use the same figure of the owner who owns nothing, which marks it as a convention of the patron's praise rather than a fact about either man.

note: 127 sets Ay's emptied palace against the cities of drum-owning kings who eat alone, give nothing and lose their fame; Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, though they hold crores.
teaches: The Kural's paradox that unshared wealth is poverty is shown in 127 from the other side, a bare palace that is rich in fame, so the pair gives both halves of one reckoning: the miser's full store is empty and the giver's empty hall is full.

note: 134 rejects as a merchant of virtue anyone who gives because what is done in this life serves the next; Naladiyar 95 tells the giver to give with an eye to the next world and this one (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் நோக்கி).
teaches: The Naladiyar's advice is the very motive the Sangam poet holds up for scorn, which shows that giving for the next birth was a live doctrine both poets knew, and that the older praise poetry judged it a lesser reason than custom and honour.

note: 134 says Ay does not give as a trade for the next world but because it is the path of the worthy; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: Both refuse to found giving on reward hereafter, but they put different things in its place: the Kural a bare judgment that giving is good, the Purananuru the example of the worthy, so the same denial could rest either on principle or on custom.

note: 136 argues that those who give to the bard give to others and those who give to others give to themselves; Kural 221 says only giving to the destitute is giving and all else is a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை).
teaches: The starving bard is exactly the Kural's destitute recipient, yet he argues that such giving does come back to the giver, so the Kural's line between true gift and loan was drawn against an older view in which even giving to the poor was defended by its return.

note: 139 urges the lord of Nanjil to give now, since he does not fear death for his king and a battle may come any day; Naladiyar 5 says not to hold back a gift thinking it can be given later, since Death drags all away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's general reason for giving now, the certainty of death, appears in 139 as a bard's practical argument tied to the warrior patron's own courage, which shows how the moralist's maxim was already a working plea in the bard's trade.
audit_text_issue: Lines 1-4 and 11 are compressed; ஈதல் ஆனான் is read as 'does not cease giving'. | Line 11 ஈதல் ஆனான் வேந்தே is hard to construe; the reading does not depend on it.

note: 123 counts Malayan's chariots as more than the raindrops on Mullur; 129 counts Ay's elephants against the stars of a sky with no dark patch.
teaches: Kapilar and Mudamosiyar measure gifts against a natural multitude, but Mudamosiyar adds a condition the real sky fails, so the second poet sharpens the formula by saying nature itself falls short of the count.

note: 141 says Pekan's giving does not look to the next world (மறுமை நோக்கின்றோ அன்றே) but to others' want; Kural 222 says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Kural's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, is already the bards' test of a true patron, and 141 adds the positive motive the couplet leaves unstated: the giver looks at the receiver's want, as the useless gift to the peacock proves.

note: 141 cites the cloak given to the peacock as proof that Pekan gives without calculation; 145 cites the same cloak (படாஅம் ஈத்த) to plead for his abandoned wife.
teaches: The peacock story served the bards both ways: as praise of pure giving in 141 and as leverage in 145, where a patron famous for pitying a bird is shamed into pitying his wife, so a patron's legend could be used against him.

note: Both liken giving to rain; Kural 211 makes the rain a duty that asks no return, while 142 notes that rain also wastes itself on salt land and calls Pekan's giving கொடைமடம், folly.
teaches: The Kural keeps only the dutiful side of the rain image, but the Purananuru poet saw its waste as well, so the rain figure for generosity carried an admitted cost of indiscrimination that the maxim leaves out.

note: 143 asks who the weeping woman at the door was (யார்கொல் அளியள்) without answering; 144 tells the same kind of scene and lets the woman answer that she is no kin of Pekan's and that he goes to another woman.
teaches: Read in sequence, the Pekan poems work as a cycle in which each poet adds what the last withheld: Kapilar leaves the woman unnamed, Paranar gives her a voice and names the cause, so the reproach of a patron was built up by several poets in turn.

note: Paranar rebukes Pekan in 144 for leaving his wife for another woman; Paranar in Akananuru 262 has a lover compare his beloved's fragrance to Pekan's rain-cloud hill (வண்மகிழ்ப் பேகன் கொண்டல் மாமலை).
teaches: The same poet uses Pekan's hill as a sweet image of union in akam while rebuking Pekan's own broken marriage in puram, so the patron's name entered akam similes as pure fame, cleansed of the scandal the puram poems record.

note: In 150 a strong-bowed hunter feeds the poet, gives his chain and will not tell his name, and is Nalli; in 152 a hunter who killed five beasts with one arrow is abashed when hailed as king, gives the meat of his kill, and is Ori.
teaches: Two poets tell the same scene of a chieftain met as an unnamed hunter in the forest who feeds the bard from his kill, so the incognito hunter-giver was a recognised type of patron story, in which the gift is proved genuine by being given before the giver is known.

note: Akananuru 238 names Nalli for rain-like giving of chariots and elephants to suppliants (மழைசுரந் தன்ன ஈகை) as a simile's backdrop; 150 tells one of his gifts in full, a chain from his chest given to a ragged poet in the forest.
teaches: The akam epithet compresses into a formula of chariots and elephants a fame that the puram poem shows was made of personal, unannounced gifts, so the akam poet's shorthand assumes hearers who knew stories like 150.

note: 151 praises the house of Kandeerakkon, where women give she-elephants when the lord is away; 150 shows Nalli, whom the colophons call Kandeerakkon, giving while concealing his name.
teaches: Both poems praise this house for giving that does not wait on the lord being seen as giver, by his women in his absence or by himself unnamed, so the Kandeera fame was for giving as a household habit, not a court performance.

note: 151 explains a snub: the poets shunned the hill of Nannan's kin because of a door shut against singers; Akananuru 152 praises Nannan for famous giving, flinging elephants (இசைநல் ஈகைக் களிறுவீசு). On the reading that the same line of Nannan is meant, the two reputations are incompatible.
teaches: Whether one Nannan or two, the name carried opposite reputations for giving in the two anthologies, which shows that a patron's fame among bards was contested and could be undone by one shut door.

note: 149 says Nalli's giving made the bards forget the hours of their modes; 153 says Ori's gifts made the troupe stop dancing and singing, since they were no longer hungry.
teaches: Two poets praise two patrons with the same joke, that plenty spoils the performer's craft, which shows that the bards themselves saw their art as driven by need and counted its loss as the fullest proof of a gift.

note: 154 makes asking for a little water from someone known the natural image for seeking out the generous; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the greatest degradation of the tongue. On the plain reading the same act is natural in one and shameful in the other.
teaches: The bard and the moralist used the same smallest request in opposite ways: for the poet it shows that seeking the generous is as natural as thirst, for the Kural it shows that no request is small enough to be clean, though 154 itself concedes that asking is hard (இரத்தலோ அரிதே).

note: 154 says the thirsty by the sea ask a known person for a little water; 204 says the thirsty do not drink from the great sea but find many paths to drinking water, even if muddied by cattle.
teaches: The sea that cannot quench thirst was a shared figure for great but useless wealth, and the two poets turn it differently: 154 uses it to explain why poets pass by kings, 204 to say a refused seeker should go elsewhere without blaming the giver.

note: 157 counts among Erai's virtues being ashamed at others' destitution (பிறர் கையறவு தான் நாணுதல்); Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace as for their own the dwelling of shame.
teaches: The Kural's widened shame, felt for what others suffer, appears first as a chief's virtue praised by a woman poet of his hill, where its object is concretely other people's want rather than their disgrace in general.

note: 158 lists Malaiyan (who rode Kari) and Ori among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras (ஓரிக் கொன்று சேரலர்க்கு ஈத்த).
teaches: The canon of the seven givers sets side by side two men one of whom killed the other, so the list honours giving alone and is silent about the wars among the givers, which the akam poet remembers in a simile.

note: 158 names 'Ori of the strong bow who ruled Kolli' (கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரி) in one line; 152 tells the hunt in which his single arrow passed through five beasts and the gifts he gave the bards.
teaches: The epithet in the roll-call condenses an exploit that 152 tells whole, so the list of seven assumed an audience that knew the separate poems on each giver.

note: 159 will refuse an elephant given grudgingly and take a kunri seed given gladly; Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural names the asker's joy at a gift without contempt; 159 turns it into a rule of conduct for the asker, who must refuse a grudging gift even while his family starves, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard could accept at all.

note: Kural 1061 says not asking even from those who give gladly is worth ten million times more; 159 treats asking a glad giver as honourable and refuses only the grudging gift.
teaches: The bard's code and the Kural's draw the line of dignity in different places: for the bard the giver's gladness makes asking clean, for the Kural even the gladdest giver does not, so the Kural's chapter on the dread of asking rejects the very compromise the parisil poems lived by.

note: 160 and 164, by different poets to the same Kumanan, both show the poet's child sucking his mother's milkless breast and crying (வறுமுலை), with empty cooking pots.
teaches: Two poets bring Kumanan the same picture of the child at the dry breast, so the starving household was a set piece of the parisil kadaanilai addressed to this patron, not one poet's private confession.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:160 line 21 வருங்கலம் is probably வறுங்கலம், the reading the note's 'empty pots' depends on.

note: 160 asks to be sent off quickly (வல்லே விடுதல் வேண்டுவல்); Naladiyar 111 says keeping a seeker waiting till hope dies is worse than ingratitude.
teaches: The Naladiyar faults delay as the giver's breach of truth; 160 shows what the delay costs at the other end, a mother distracting a hungry child at home, which is why the bard asks for speed before size.
audit_text_issue: Possible misprints at lines 6, 10, 14 and 21 (குனிப்ப/குளிப்ப, கோடின்றாக/கேடின்றாக, நல்குவை/நல்குவன், வருங்கலம்/வறுங்கலம்).

note: In 161 Perunchiththiranar asks Kumanan for a tusker to ride home on so that ungiving kings are shamed; in 162 the same poet ties an elephant to Ilaveliman's guard tree and leaves, saying givers exist elsewhere.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the gift elephant doing what 161 promised: the bard's reward from one patron becomes a public rebuke staked at the door of a patron who failed him, so giving among chiefs was a contest the bards could stage.

note: 162 says to Ilaveliman: see that askers exist and that givers exist; Kural 1055 says askers stand before others because there are people in the world who do not withhold.
teaches: The Kural explains asking by the existence of givers in general; 162 uses that same general truth as a weapon against one particular chief, so the principle that kept the asker's dignity also let him walk away from a mean patron.

note: In 159 the poet pictures his wife boiling unsalted greens and his starving household as the reason for his plea to Kumanan; in 163 he tells her to give Kumanan's gift away to all, without consulting him.
teaches: The household whose hunger was the bard's argument for the gift becomes, as soon as the gift arrives, a giver to its own kin and creditors, so the bard's reward was expected to circulate, not to be saved.

note: Both petitions to Kumanan picture the bard's child sucking a breast dry for want of food (160 lines 17 to 19; 164 lines 3 to 5).
teaches: Two different poets press Kumanan with the same picture of the child at the milkless breast, which shows it was a set argument of the plea for a gift (பரிசில் கடாநிலை) rather than one poet's private report.
audit_text_issue: Purananuru 160 has misprint candidates at lines 6, 10, 14 and 21, which do not affect the breast image. | 160 has misprint candidates at lines 6, 10, 14, 21 (not in the breast lines).

note: 160 shows Kumanan at Muthiram flinging away gold vessels so the bards' troupe may not fail; 165 shows a giver who has lost his land offering his own head because a disappointed bard is worse to him than that loss.
teaches: Set beside 160's lavish lord in his own hill, 165 tests the same habit of giving after the land is gone: what remains to give is the self, so the giver's fame survives his loss of wealth.
audit_text_issue: 160 has four variant lines; at line 10 கோடின்றாக against கேடின்றாக bears on 'may not fail'

note: Kural 230 says death is the bitterest thing, yet sweet when one cannot give; in 165 the giver says a bard going away disappointed is worse than losing his country and gives his head.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is a figure of speech in a couplet; 165 gives it a narrative in which a dispossessed chief literally prefers death to failing a bard, so the maxim had a heroic story behind it.

note: 165 opens: those who wished to last in an unlasting world set up their fame and died; Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame.
teaches: The Kural states the rule abstractly; 165 places it as the premise of a gift poem and adds its converse, that the ungiving rich are forgotten, so fame here is something the bard both records and withholds.

note: Kural 776 makes the day without a noble wound a wasted day; 167 grants the king's scars are sweet to hear of but says they are harsh to see, and the enemies' whole skins sweet to see.
teaches: Where the Kural counts the wound only as the warrior's own ledger of worth, 167 adds the onlooker's split response, so the wound's value lies in report and fame, not in how it looks.

note: Both name the Kosar of many spears: in Akananuru 113 as loyal guards whose rich land stands for the heroine's lover, in 169 as young men practising spear throws at a murukku post, the simile for Pittan's strength.
teaches: The Kosar were a byword for spear-skill and fidelity known to both genres: the akam poet borrows their loyalty to measure a lover's land, the puram poet their training post to measure a chief, so their fame served as a ready image in both kinds of poem.

note: Both poems bring in the dark-handed smith (கருங்கைக் கொல்லன்): in 170 the anvil that takes his hammer is the chief facing his foes; in 180 the poor chief asks his town's smith to forge a spear to feed the bards.
teaches: The smith's forge stands in both poems for the link between fighting and giving: 170 makes the chief the anvil that wears out his enemies, and 180 shows the spear made there as the source of the bards' meal.

note: Kural 227 calls hunger a fierce disease (பசியென்னும் தீப்பிணி) that will not touch one who shares food; 173 calls Pannan the physician of the disease of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்).
teaches: Both books treat hunger as a disease, but the Kural says sharing protects the sharer while 173 makes the giver the healer of other people's hunger, so the image moves from the giver's safety to the hungry crowd's cure.

note: In 70 a bard steering another to Killi Valavan names on the way the village of Pannan the open-handed; in 173 a Chola king, Killi Valavan by the colophon, wishes his own years on Pannan and calls him the physician of hunger.
teaches: 70 gives Pannan as a landmark of generosity on the road to the king; 173 has a king himself defer to that small-village chief, so Pannan's fame for giving stood in the anthology beside, not beneath, a crowned king's.

note: 123 is Kapilar's praise of Malayan, whose gifts outnumber the raindrops on Mullur; 174 refers to Mullur as the hill truthful-tongued Kapilan sang and praises a later chief of the same house.
teaches: 174 cites the earlier poem by its poet and place, which shows that a Sangam poet could rest a patron's fame on a famous song already in circulation, and that Mullur's renown was itself made by Kapilar's verse.

note: Both use the formula of the Moriyar with sky-touching umbrellas whose chariot wheels cut a pass through rock (Akananuru 69 lines 10 to 12; 175 lines 6 to 8).
teaches: The same Mauryan landmark serves akam as the far, dangerous road the hero crosses for wealth and puram as a figure for the fixed, unfailing care of a patron, so the formula's sense came from the poem it was set in, not from the place.

note: Kural 107 says one remembers the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow for seven births; 175 says the poet will forget Athanungan only when he forgets himself, when life leaves the body.
teaches: The Kural stretches gratitude across seven births, while the Purananuru poet bounds it by this one life and locates it in his body, which shows the older poem's gratitude making no claim on rebirth.

note: 109 says Parambu's springs are as many as the stars and that it cannot be starved; 176 uses those cool clear springs as what people living beside them did not value.
teaches: 109 offers the springs as proof that Pari's hill never fails, and 176 turns that very constancy into a lesson on neglect: what is always at hand, a spring or a near patron, goes unvalued.

note: 158 lists the seven great givers who are dead and turns to Kumanan as the one left; 179 opens with the generous of the earth dead and the bard's bowl upturned, and names Nagan of Nalai as the one who will fill it.
teaches: After the seven givers died became a reusable opening: 158 applies it to a hill king and 179 to a Pandya's soldier, so a lesser patron could be raised into the line of the great givers by the same formula.

note: 167 says the king's sword-scarred body is sweet to hear of and harsh to see; 180 describes a chief whose body is all scars, who has no wealth and gives by having a spear forged.
teaches: 167 values the scars as fame; 180 shows them as the price of the bards' meal, since a chief without treasure gives only by fighting, so the wound in puram poetry is both glory and the means of giving.

note: Naladiyar 159 says the excellent honour a frequent visitor each time they see him; 171 says Kotran gives whether we come today, later or every day, never saying he gave before.
teaches: The Naladiyar states as a mark of character what 171 records of one chief's practice with bards, so the later maxim about the frequent visitor had its model in the patron who gave daily without reproach.

note: Naladiyar 100 says the word 'they gave' is heard through the three worlds, further than drum or thunder; 168 says bards praise Kotran across the Tamil land every day, shaming kings who do not give.
teaches: 168 shows the mechanism the Naladiyar leaves out: the fame of giving travels because the bards who received the gifts carry it, and it is aimed at the kings who did not give.

note: Both say the world stands because of a certain kind of person: 182 names those who strive for others, Kural 996 those of courtesy (பண்புடையார்), without whom it would sink into the earth.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a two-line rule what the Pandya prince builds as a list of concrete refusals, so the reader of the Kural can see which deeds (not eating alone, dying for honour, refusing blame-tainted gain) its abstract பண்பு was taken to mean.

note: 182 opens its catalogue with not eating alone even the nectar of the gods; Kural 322 makes sharing one's food the chief of all virtues.
teaches: Sharing food heads the list in both books, which shows that in early Tamil ethics the shared meal, not an inner disposition, was the first test of a good person.

note: 182 opens உண்டால் அம்ம, இவ்வுலகம் (the world exists, indeed) and 194 says இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம் (the world is harsh, indeed): the same exclamation over the same world.
teaches: Two poets use one formula to say opposite things about this world, and each turns it to action, so the formula shows the anthology arguing with itself: the world is kept going by the selfless in 182, and is bitter yet must be met by seeking good in 194.

note: Both rank learning above birth: in 183 a man of the highest order defers to a learned man of the lowest, and Kural 409 says the unlearned high-born lack the worth of the learned low-born.
teaches: The Kural's maxim was already a king's teaching in the Purananuru, where Nedunchezhiyan keeps the four orders by name and lets learning reverse them, so neither text abolishes birth rank: both use it as the measure that learning overturns.

note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

note: Kural 552 calls the sceptre-holder's demand a robber's demand at spear-point; 184 likens the greedy king to an elephant loose in a field.
teaches: The Kural condemns excess levy from the subject's side as robbery, while Pisirandhaiyar argues from the king's side that grabbing wastes more than it yields and leaves the king himself unfed, so the same rule is given both a moral and a prudential ground.

note: Kural 542 sets the world's dependence on the sky beside the people's dependence on the sceptre; 186 denies rice and water the name of life and gives it to the king alone.
teaches: The Kural keeps rain and rule as parallel supports, but Mosikeeranar ranks the king above food and water and then turns the claim into the king's own duty to know it, so the pair shows the same dependence read once as praise and once as a burden laid on the ruler.

note: Kural 737 defines a country by its limbs: waters, a well-placed hill, the water from it and a strong fort. 187 says no kind of ground, plain, forest, low or high, makes a land good, only the goodness of its men. On the reading that both answer what makes a land good, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the land lists natural and built assets, while Avvaiyar dismisses terrain altogether, so a reader sees two answers to one question, resources or people, and that the Purananuru gave the moral answer before the treatise gave the material one.

note: 186 says the world lives by its king; 187 says a land is good wherever its men are good, naming no king.
teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the two maxims locate the source of a land's well-being in different hands, the ruler in 186 and the men at large in 187, so the reader sees that Sangam counsel did not rest the realm on the king alone.

note: Both turn on a small child's hand in the food: Kural 64 says gruel stirred by children's small hands is sweeter than nectar; 188 lists the child's touching, biting, stirring and scattering of ghee rice.
teaches: The Kural makes the image a measure of sweetness, while the Pandya king makes its absence a verdict that a rich man's feasting life is profitless, so one scene serves as delight in one book and as the test of a wasted life in the other.

note: 189 says the use of wealth is giving and whoever means to enjoy it alone loses much; Naladiyar 9 says the man who neither eats, gives nor relieves his kin but guards his wealth is counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Both declare kept wealth already lost, but for different reasons: Nakkeerar from the fixed measure one body can eat and wear, the Naladiyar from the miser's failure in every use, so the pair gives the conclusion one ground in the body and one in duty.

note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who accept good when it comes grieve when it does not; 192 neither rejoices that life is sweet nor calls it bitter, because a life follows its order.
teaches: Both ground equanimity on an order the person does not control, but the Kural names it ஊழ் and argues, while Kaniyan gives the picture of a raft carried on a flood, so the abstract fate of the Kural is given an image of how it works.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why anyone stays unlearned; 192 says every town is ours and everyone our kin, with no condition of learning.
teaches: The Kural makes belonging everywhere a reward of learning, while Kaniyan makes it a consequence of seeing that good and ill are not given by others, so the pair shows the same cosmopolitan claim earned once by study and once by insight.

note: 194 declares இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம், this world is harsh, and blames its maker; 192 says we do not in disgust call life bitter (இன்னாது என்றலும் இலமே). Read as judgments of the world, they are incompatible.
teaches: One anthology holds both the verdict that the world is bitter and the refusal to pass that verdict, using the same word இன்னாது, so the reader sees that Purananuru ethics offered two stances to grief, protest and equanimity, rather than one doctrine.

note: Both set a wedding drum against a funeral drum. Naladiyar 23 draws the lesson that the worthy hold to the way of escape; 194 tells those who know the world's nature to look for what is sweet (இனிய காண்க). On the reading that இனிய means good deeds in this life, the two conclusions diverge.
teaches: The same sight of joy and mourning side by side leads the Naladiyar to renunciation and the Purananuru poet to seeking good within the world, which shows the later didactic book reusing a Sangam image for a different, ascetic conclusion.

note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the death rattle stops the tongue; 195, facing old men who have done no good, asks at least that they refrain from harm.
teaches: The Kural's urgency assumes one can still act well, while the Purananuru poet sets a floor for those who will not, so the pair shows that early Tamil counsel allowed abstaining from harm to count as a road to the good when doing good had failed.

note: Kural 1051 says if those worth asking withhold, the blame is theirs; 196 says a false promise or a false refusal lessens the giver's fame.
teaches: The Kural states as a rule that withholding shames the giver, not the asker, and Avur Moolankizhar applies it to a named king's delay, so the rule had been used as a poet's weapon before it became a maxim.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: Kural 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than the poverty of the good; 197 says the poet thinks nothing of the riches of the unfeeling and thinks of the poverty of the wise with joy.
teaches: The Kural's comparison is spoken by a poet to a Chola king's face in the Purananuru, which shows that the maxim's ranking of the wise poor over the ignorant rich was first a bard's claim on his own dignity before a patron.

note: 192 ends பெரியோரை வியத்தலும் இலமே, we do not marvel at the great; 197 says the poet does not marvel (வியத்தலோ இலமே) at kings' umbrella wealth but at small chiefs who know how to treat poets.
teaches: Kaniyan's refusal to admire the great is a philosophical stance, and Kumaranar turns it into a bard's practice before a king, choosing whom to admire by conduct, so the pair shows a cosmological equanimity becoming a social rule of honour.

note: Naladiyar 206 says saltless millet gruel among one's own is sweeter than milk rice from strangers' hands; 197 prizes the small chief's greens and varagu rice given with regard over kings' wealth.
teaches: Both value a poor meal for the regard it is given with, but the Naladiyar finds that regard among kin while the Purananuru finds it in a patron who knows a poet's worth, so the pair shows the bard's patron standing where the family stands in the later book.

note: 198 has the poet long for the king's grace like the bird that longs for a raindrop; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return daily to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: Both poems make the suppliant a bird, but 198's lone bird waits for a drop and begs not to be forgotten, while 199's flock returns without shame to a sure tree, so the pair shows the bard's two postures, anxious waiting and confident return, and what decides between them is the patron.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

note: 201 offers Pari's daughters to Irungovel with praise of his lineage; 202, after the refusal, recalls that his ancestors' Araiyam fell for scorning a poet and withdraws the offer.
teaches: Read as a pair, the two poems show the bard's praise of lineage working as a bargaining position: the same forty-nine generations that 201 flatters become in 202 a house with a known record of ruin for slighting poets.

note: 201 is spoken after Pari's fall, with his daughters taken to another chief; Akananuru 78 measures the heroine's brow by the flowers of the pool of Pari, the giver who drove off kings (வேந்தர்ஓட்டிய).
teaches: The akam poet keeps Pari as the victor whose hill still blooms, while Kapilar's poem records the aftermath in which his daughters need a protector, so akam fixes a hero at his height that puram follows past his death.

note: 202 closes by wishing Irungovel's spear victory; Akananuru 36 lists Irungo Venman among the seven defeated in one day by Chezhiyan at Alankanam.
teaches: If the two name the same house, the akam friend's list of fallen kings shows the defeat that Kapilar's parting blessing does not foresee, and shows akam poets drawing on puram battle-lists as common knowledge to scale a quarrel.
audit_text_issue: 202 marked uncertain; கழாஅத் தலையை read as a name by the marker.

note: 203 calls it cruel (இன்னாது) for a patron to refuse a returning bard with 'you took before'; Kural 224 says being asked is itself painful (இன்னாது) to the giver until he sees the asker's glad face.
teaches: The same word marks the pain of the asking moment from opposite sides, the giver's in the Kural and the refused bard's in 203, so the couplet's candour about the giver's discomfort is answered by a poet who names what that discomfort costs the asker.

note: 204 ranks four acts: asking low, refusing lower, giving high, refusing a gift higher; Kural 222 ranks two: taking is bad even on a good path, giving good even without heaven.
teaches: The Sangam poet's ladder adds a rung the Kural lacks, the refusal of what is offered, which shows that the Kural's verdict against taking had a heroic form in which the proud receiver outranks the giver.

note: 204 says those who come in hope blame the omens and the hour, never the patron; Kural 1051 says that when the worthy withhold, the blame is theirs and not the asker's. On the plain reading the two place the blame for a refused request in incompatible places.
teaches: The bard's courtesy in 204 is a deliberate refusal to lay the blame that the Kural says belongs to the withholder, so the poem shows the decorum that kept a disappointed poet in a patron's favour against the moral rule.

note: 204 praises Ori as a giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit; Akananuru 209 names Kari of Mullur, who killed Ori of the strong bow and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
teaches: The puram poem preserves Ori as a living patron while the akam friend cites his killing as a famous deed of another chief, so one man's fame survives in the anthologies as both a patron's praise and a rival's trophy.

note: 205, by Perunthalai Sathanar, praises the hunter lord of Kodai whose bards never leave without chariots and elephants; Akananuru 13, by the same poet, names the Kodai lord who gives to suppliants without limit (வரைநிலை இன்றி) except the captured elephant.
teaches: The same poet turns his patron's giving into an akam measure of what the hero would forgo by leaving, and his akam line keeps a detail the puram poem omits, that one gift, the captured elephant, was only promised by word.

note: 205 says the bard does not want even the three kings' gifts if given without regard (பெட்பின்றி); Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural states the receiver's joy at a gift given without contempt; 205 turns it into a condition of acceptance, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard would take the gift at all, not only how he felt about it.

note: 206 has Avvai leave Anji's gate saying that wherever bards go, there is rice; 207 has Perunchithiranar tell his heart that the world is wide and providers many for those who want honour.
teaches: Two poets leaving two patrons reach the same exit, the claim that the world is wide, which shows it was a stock defence of the bard's honour against a patron's slight, not one poet's pique.

note: 206 shows the bard leaving in pride when kept waiting at the gate; Kural 1060 says the asker should not be angry when refused, since his own want shows wealth is hard to come by.
teaches: Avvai is not refused a gift but denied recognition at the gate, so the pair separates two cases the Kural's counsel of patience joins: want may excuse a refusal, but the bards held that a slight to their rank was not to be borne.

note: 207 rejects a gift that does not make the heart glad and leaves the face fallen (அகம்நக வாரா முகன்அழி); Kural 786 says friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship, only that which makes the heart smile.
teaches: The Kural's pair of face and heart (முகநக, அகநக) already stands in a bard's test of a gift, so the measure the Kural applies to friendship was first a poet's measure of patronage.

note: 208 says the poet is not a trading bard (வாணிகப் பரிசிலன்) for a gift given unseen; 134 says Ay is not a merchant of virtue (அறவிலை வணிகன்) who gives for a return in the next life.
teaches: The figure of the trader is used against both sides of the gift: a giver who expects return and a receiver who takes without recognition are both merchants, so the ideal gift was one where neither party was trading.

note: 209 likens the bard to birds that leave a fruit tree gone bare; 207 says only the faint-hearted pine for a hard fruit that will never ripen.
teaches: Both poets cast the patron as a fruit tree, but 209 blames the tree for being bare while 207 blames the bard for waiting on unripe fruit, so the same image could carry a reproach to the patron or a resolve to leave him.
audit_text_issue: 209 line 10 has an edition variant (புள்ளிமை for புள்ளினம்; missing in one edition).

note: Both poems are Perunkunrur Kizhar's to Kudakko Cheral Irumporai; 210 quotes the wife who thinks him dead, 211 ends at the house where the rat has died and the son has forgotten the breast.
teaches: The two poems bring the bard's household to the king's court in two ways, the wife's speech in 210 and the bare house in 211, which shows the poor home used as evidence in a bard's case against a patron who kept him waiting.

note: 211 tells of a patron who showed the gift as if in hand and then stood by a lie; Kural 1067 begs all who beg not to ask of those who conceal.
teaches: The Kural's advice not to beg from concealers is given from outside; 211 shows from inside what the bard does when the advice comes too late, shaming by praise (நாணக் கூறி) as his only remedy.

note: 212, by Pisirandhaiyar, praises Kopperuncholan through the toddy, tortoise and eel of his land; 215, by the king, praises Pisirandhaiyar through the varagu, curd and tamarind gruel of his.
teaches: Each friend praises the other through the food of the other's home, the Chola's rich marutham fare and the Pandya-country poet's plain mullai fare, so the friendship poems are built as a matched pair across two kingdoms.

note: 213 counsels the king that a war with those who rose against him (traditionally his sons) is lost whichever side wins; Kural 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed, holds ruin.
teaches: The Kural asserts that enmity within brings ruin; 213 gives the reason in a single case, since in a war inside the house the king loses his heirs if he wins and his honour if he loses.

note: 214 urges good deeds on the reckoning that they may win the world without deeds, release from birth, or fame; 134 praises Ay for not being a merchant of virtue who holds that what is done here serves the next life. On the plain reading 214 recommends the very motive 134 scorns.
teaches: The same anthology holds a king reasoning openly about the returns of merit and a poet scorning such reasoning in a patron, so the Sangam poets did not share one view of whether a deed's next-world return was a fit motive.

note: 214 reasons that even if there is no joy beyond, good deeds may end rebirth or leave fame; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: Both test good conduct on the supposition that there is no heaven, but the Kural rests there while the king reaches for a further reward, release or fame, so the pair shows two ways of answering doubt about the next world.

note: 215 says Pisiron may stay away in prosperity but will not stay away in trouble; Naladiyar 238 is an oath to rush to a friend in distress and put one's life in his hands.
teaches: The Naladiyar's oath is a figure of speech, but in the tradition this chapter records the friend did come to share the king's death, so the puram poems supply a case in which the oath was taken literally.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: 216 has the king tell doubters that his unseen friend will come; 217 marvels that the king said 'he will come' and the friend came without fail.
teaches: The second poem is the fulfilment of the first, and it moves the wonder from the friend's faith to the king's foresight, so the pair shows the lament praising the dead man for having judged a friend rightly.

note: 218 says the worthy join the worthy as gems from distant places meet in one jewel; Naladiyar 236 says the water-lily and the kuvalai grow in one pool, yet the small do not equal the great.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows that nearness does not make likeness and the Sangam poem that distance does not prevent it, so together they make nature, not place, the ground of fellowship.

note: 218 says the worthy fall to the side of the worthy; 219 tells the fasting king that many have already sat with him in his resolve.
teaches: The maxim of 218 becomes in 219 a crowd on the river island, which shows that the lament poems treat the number of those who joined the king's death as the measure of his worth.

note: 212 shows Kopperuncholan's land of festivals and his daily gift of laughter; 220 shows the assembly of the old town empty after Killi has gone.
teaches: Read together, the two poems bracket the Chola's life in the chapter, the festive court of 212 and the empty hall of 220, so the sequence of the anthology itself tells the story of the king's death.

note: Kural 771 boasts that many who stood against the speaker's lord now stand as stones (கல்நின் றவர்); 221 ends with the generous patron himself become a hero-stone (நடுகல் ஆயினன் புரவலன்), mourned by poets.
teaches: In the Kural the hero-stone is the fate a warrior threatens on his enemies, while in 221 it is the end of the patron the poets loved, so the same stone that marks a foe's defeat also marks the giver's fame, and the boast of 771 is one side of a monument that kaiyarunilai shows from the other.

note: Akananuru 55 recalls Cheralathan sitting facing north (வான்வடக் கிருந்தென) after his wound at Venni and the worthies who went with him to the other world; in 222 the poet reproaches his king for telling him to come only after his son was born.
teaches: The akam simile shows that companions dying with a king who sat facing north was a known and honoured act, which explains why being told to wait for a son's birth is felt in 222 as a lack of love: the friend was barred from an honour the custom gave him.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as a bond that never curtails the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை); 223 says the king, even as a hero-stone, gives room to friends of old intimacy (கிழமைத் தொன்னட் புடையார்) who come to him.
teaches: The Kural's definition is carried past death in 223: the claim of intimacy that a friend may exercise unasked includes the right to follow the king into death, and the stone honours it by making room, so pazhaimai is tested at its extreme.
audit_text_issue: 223 line 2 (தலைப்போ கன்மையிற் சிறுவழி மடங்கி) is compressed and unclear.

note: 224 mourns the king of the colophon, Karikalan, listing his battles, feeding of bards and sacrifice; Akananuru 55 recalls Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni, after which the defeated Cheral sat facing north and worthies died with him.
teaches: Karikalan is remembered in the akam simile through the mourning his victory caused in the defeated court, and in 224 through his own women's stripped ornaments, so the same king stands in the corpus at both ends of the grief that war produces.

note: Line 7 of 225 and line 13 of 237 are the same line, கள்ளி போகிய களரியம் பறந்தலை, naming the cremation ground where Nalankilli's strength now lies and where the young hero perished.
teaches: Two poets mourning different patrons reach for the identical line for the burning ground, which shows that kaiyarunilai drew on a shared stock of formulas, and that what made each poem particular was what it set on that ground: an army's might in 225, a bard's lost hope in 237.
audit_text_issue: 225 lines 13 to 14 hard, marker flagged uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 20 pictures merciless Death roaming for its victims and seizing even the unborn while the mother wails; 226 says Death could not have taken Valavan by rage or force and must have begged him like a bard.
teaches: On the Naladiyar's account no one escapes a Death that takes by force, while 226 claims that this king was beyond Death's force and fell only to his own generosity, so the bardic lament denies the very powerlessness before Death that the moralist uses to urge virtue.

note: 228 asks how a potter could make an urn big enough for Valavan, with the earth for his wheel and a mountain for clay; 231 says that whether Anji's pyre is low or reaches the sky, his fame will not perish.
teaches: 228 measures the king's greatness by the size of the funeral vessel it would need, while 231 declares the size of the pyre irrelevant to fame, so the two poems show the funeral rite being used both as the measure of greatness and as the thing greatness escapes.

note: 227 tells Death it has cooked and eaten its seed (வித்துஅட்டு உண்டனை) in taking Valavan; 230 likens Death to a failing farmer who eats his seed (வித்து உண்டாஅங்கு) in taking Ezhini.
teaches: Two poets on different kings make the same argument through the seed image, that a slain warrior was the source of Death's future harvest of enemies, which shows that taunting Death with its own loss was a recognised move in kaiyarunilai and not one poet's conceit.
audit_text_issue: 230 colophon thurai reads கையுறுநிலை, a misprint for கையறுநிலை.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except unmatched renown; 231 says Anji's fame will not perish whether his pyre shrinks or rises to the sky.
teaches: Avvai's poem gives the Kural's general claim its occasion: fame is undying precisely at the pyre, where everything else of the man is being burned, so the maxim's 'nothing else stands' is shown in the act of the body's ending.

note: In 235 Avvai remembers Anji sharing his toddy with her; in 232 she pictures toddy poured from a small cup on his hero-stone and asks whether he who refused a whole country will accept it.
teaches: The toddy he once shared with his poet returns in 232 as a funeral offering to his stone, so the rite reverses their old roles (now she gives and he must receive), which is why Avvai cannot believe he will accept it.

note: 233 refuses the dawn report of spear wounds on the chest of Evvi, leader of the bards' families; Akananuru 115 uses the bards who, in the battle where Evvi fell (எவ்வி வீழ்ந்த செருவில் பாணர்), broke off the curved necks of their lutes, as a simile for konrai pods on a desert path.
teaches: The akam poet assumes his hearers know that bards mourned Evvi by breaking their lutes, so the death the puram poet cannot bring himself to believe became, in the akam tradition, a fixed public memory usable as a passing image of curved pods.

note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; 234 grieves that Evvi, who always ate with many at a gate open to the world, is now fed alone a small rice ball on grass by his wife.
teaches: The Kural condemns solitary eating as the miser's choice, and 234 shows death forcing that very condition on the most open-handed host, so the bitterness the Kural assigns to the hoarder becomes, in the lament, the injury done to the giver by his funeral rite.

note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of one who gives nothing to a beautiful woman growing old alone; 235 ends by likening the many lives that die without giving to pakanrai flowers that wither unworn.
teaches: Both books picture what is not given as beauty that no one enjoys, but Avvai moves the image from the miser's wealth to the miser's life and sets it against a giver who has just died, so the waste is measured by the loss of one who did give.

note: Kapilar says Pari told him 'stay behind' (ஒழிக) and would not let him come; Pothiyar says the king left him here (என்இவண் ஒழித்த) telling him to come only after his son's birth.
teaches: Two poets of different patrons voice the same grievance, that the patron forbade his friend to follow him in death, and Kapilar resolves it differently, by asking fate for the next birth, so the pair shows that kaiyarunilai had a recognised place for the friend refused the right to die with his lord.

note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; 237 says a tiger that misses the elephant it stalked will not stalk a rat, and the poet resolves to seek great gifts.
teaches: The Kural's warrior maxim about aiming high is used in 237 by a bard to turn from mourning to his next patron, so the ethic of the great target governed the bard's choice of patron as well as the soldier's choice of foe.

note: Kural 922 says not to drink toddy, and that only those who do not care to be counted by the worthy should; 239 lists draining jars of sweet toddy among the deeds of a man who 'did all that should be done' and so earned fame.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree about whether drinking belongs to a praiseworthy life: the Kural excludes the drinker from the esteem of the worthy, while the Purananuru lament counts the toddy jar beside justice and giving in a life complete enough to make the manner of burial indifferent.

note: 240 calls Aay Andiran never stinting singers of horses, elephants and chariots; Akananuru 152 names 'Aay's forest' after the Aay who gives elephants to all who come, skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Aay's open-handedness to name a place, while the puram poem records what followed his death, his poets scattering to other lands, so the patron's giving outlived him as a landmark in love poetry even as the household it fed dissolved.

note: Two kaiyarunilai poems on the death of Ay Andiran: 240 stays at the pyre and the scattering bards, 241 looks to the drum of the heavenly hall.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that a lament for a patron could face downward to the hungry dependents or upward to his welcome among the gods, and that the heavenly version is offered as consolation for the earthly one.

note: 241 presents Andiran's giving of chariots as what announces him in heaven; the Kural says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Kural's hypothetical answers a real habit of praise: poets like this one tied giving to a welcome in the sky, and the couplet deliberately cuts that tie so that giving no longer needs the reward.

note: Both picture old age on a staff, but the Naladiyar calls youth faulty and the wise renounce it in infancy, while 243 calls its untaught youth precious and grieves for it.
teaches: The same image of the old man on a staff serves the Jain moralist as a warning against enjoying youth and the Sangam poet as proof that youth was the best of life, so the later book is arguing against a value the older poetry held.

note: Tirumanthiram 157 calls the mourners who burn the body and bathe unjust for returning to life; 245 is a mourner who burned his wife and is appalled that he still lives.
teaches: The king's poem complicates the Tirumanthiram's charge: survival after the pyre is shown not as forgetting but as grief's own failure to kill, which the survivor feels as shame.

note: The queen of 246 refuses the widow's life of greens and alli; the widow of 248 lives it and pities the lilies that now feed her.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two poems show that the widow's diet was a known, codified life that one woman could choose to bear and another could scorn as worse than the pyre.

note: Both are filed as ஆனந்தப் பையுள: 246 gives the queen's refusal in her own voice, 247 shows a widow at the burning ground from outside, wavering.
teaches: The resolve that 246 voices without a tremor is seen in 247 from the outside as hesitation and fear for one's young life, so the same thurai holds both the heroic and the frightened face of the same choice.

note: Both name alli as the widow's food (அல்லி உணவின், அல்லிப் படுஉம்).
teaches: The repeated alli food shows a fixed sign of widowhood shared across poets, which 250 sets against the house's former feasting and 248 against the girl's lily-leaf garment.

note: The Kural likens the false ascetic to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 252 says this ascetic really was a hunter, snaring women with words, before he became one.
teaches: Both use the hunter and the snared bird for the ascetic, but in opposite order: for the Kural the hunter hides inside the ascetic, for the Sangam poet the ascetic has replaced the hunter, so the same image can accuse or praise a renunciant.

note: Two poems by the same poet on the ascetic's life: 251 sets the seducer against the ascetic at the fire, 252 names his past as hunting with a net of words.
teaches: The pair shows the poet working one contrast twice, with the second poem turning the past from the women's pining to the man's own art of capture, which makes the renunciation a giving up of skill as well as pleasure.

note: Both have the bare, pale, bangle-less hand raised among the kin (வளையில் வறுங்கை ஓச்சிக் கிளையுள்).
teaches: The near-identical line in poems by different poets shows that the widow's raised empty arm was a fixed formula of the முதுபாலை thurai, used in 253 for the wife's own shame and in 254 for the news she must carry to the mother.

note: The Kural's mother rejoices more at hearing her son called worthy than at his birth; 254's mother praises her son daily, and the speaker dreads her hearing of his death.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows the other side of the Kural's maxim: the mother whose joy rests on hearing her son praised is the one whom the word of his death will strike hardest.

note: Both are spoken by a wife alone with her husband's body in the wilds: 255 tries to move him to the hill's shade, 256 asks the potter for an urn wide enough for two.
teaches: Taken in order, the two widows move from refusing the death (walk a little, she tells the corpse) to arranging to share it, which shows the range of response that the முதுபாலை thurai held.

note: The Kural says shame turns her back on drinkers; in 258 the toddy jar is reserved for the raider as an honour before his deed.
teaches: The pairing shows that drinking was an honour of the warrior's rite (உண்டாட்டு) in the older poetry, so the Kural's chapter against liquor is rejecting a heroic custom, not only a private vice.

note: The Kural says a death that is really existence is hard to achieve save for the skilled; 260 shows the hero's body left shaking with arrows while his name passes onto the stone.
teaches: 260 gives the Kural's abstract paradox a concrete form: the 'death that lives' was a practice with a body left on the bank, a stone set in a narrow path, and a name crowned with peacock feathers.

note: 259 warns the karanthai warrior against the ambush as he chases the herd; 260 tells of a karanthai warrior who recovered the herd and died of the arrows.
teaches: Read in order, the warning of 259 and the hero-stone of 260 give the two ends of the herd-recovery: the danger seen in advance and the death it brings, which is why the recovery's praise ends at a stone.

note: 246's speaker is the queen of Bhoothapandiyan; the colophon of Akananuru 25 names Bhoothapandiyan as its poet, whose hero vows 'let my life suffer' at parting.
teaches: Through the colophons, the akam poet who wrote a lover's promise not to stay away is also the husband whose wife refused to outlive him, so the anthologies let a convention of inseparable lovers stand beside one recorded marriage.

note: Both address the dead lord's house with புல்என் றனையால் (you have become desolate) and set a widow beside it: 261 likens the house to a widow with shorn head, 250 shows the widow shorn and eating lily seeds inside it.
teaches: One formula serves two poets, and the widow sits once in a simile and once in the house, which shows that the empty hall and the widow's state were one picture of a lord's death, interchangeable as tenor and vehicle.

note: 261 likens the house to a கழிகலம் மகடூஉ with shorn head; in 280 the wife foresees becoming one of the கழிகல மகளிர் with shaven head.
teaches: In 261 the shorn widow is only an image for a ruined house; in 280 the wife speaks it of herself as her own future, so the pair shows the same stock figure moving from ornament to fate depending on who speaks.

note: 335 says the people know no god worshipped with poured paddy except the stone of the man who fell killing an elephant; 263 tells a passing bard not to go by such a stone without worship.
teaches: 335 states the creed of the hero-stone as a general fact of a small warrior land, and 263 shows it working as an obligation laid on travellers, so together they show the cult reaching beyond the dead man's village to the road.

note: Both describe the making of a hero-stone: 264's name carved, red flower garland bound with maral fibre and peacock feather; Akananuru 269's names washed, turmeric, and a karanthai garland tied with fibre on the stone by the road.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the puram rite almost item by item to fill the heroine's fear of the road, which shows that the hero-stone was a fixed, widely known ritual whose details an akam audience would recognise as danger without being told.

note: In 232 Avvaiyar asks whether the patron who would not accept a whole country will now accept toddy poured at his feather-crowned stone; in 264 the bards may still be coming to a patron who is now a stone.
teaches: Both poems turn on the reversal the stone makes in the gift relation: in 232 the giver becomes a receiver of offerings, and in 264 the receivers arrive to find no giver, so together they show that a patron's death was grieved as the end of a circuit of giving.

note: 221 ends நடுகல் ஆயினன் புரவலன் (the patron has become a hero-stone); 265 says கல்ஆ யினையே (you have become a stone) and adds that the bards' wealth went with him.
teaches: The formula 'he became a stone' is used of a crowned king in 221 and of a local cattle-defender in 265, which shows that the hero-stone honour, and the bards' claim on the dead, were not reserved for kings.

note: Kural 771 threatens enemies that many who stood before the lord now stand as stones; in 265 the stone is the hero's own, and the poet grieves that patronage and victory went with him.
teaches: The Kural's boast treats the hero-stone as the enemy's fate and a mark of the lord's might, while 265 shows the same stone from the side of those left behind, so the pair shows that the honour Valluvar's warrior wields as a threat was, for the bards, a loss of livelihood.

note: Naladiyar 287 says want takes away good nature and sharpness of mind; 266 names its poverty as அறிவுகெட நின்ற, which has ruined his understanding, and as making him hide from guests.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim that poverty destroys the mind is given here as a poet's own testimony with a concrete symptom, hiding from the guest one longed for, which shows that the loss of hospitality was felt as the loss of reason itself.

note: Naladiyar 286 says the man who cannot give to those who come hungry had better leave his village; 266 asks the king to end such poverty quickly, as a plea in the assembly is answered.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the poor host's shame his own to solve by leaving, while the Purananuru poet places the remedy on the king as a matter of justice, so the pair shows two answers to the same shame: private withdrawal and a public claim on the ruler.

note: Both are உண்டாட்டு feasts after a cattle raid: 262 orders toddy drawn and a ram killed for the returning lord, 269 shows the warrior drinking and answering the drummer's request with the sword's deed.
teaches: 262 is the feast prepared and 269 the feast in progress, and in both the drink is bound to the deed that earned it, which shows that the victory feast was a rite of reward rather than mere celebration.

note: Both set the nochchi on women's waists and on the defender's head: 271 ends with the garland bloodied and carried off by a kite, 272 with the tree's honour of crowning the man who would not yield.
teaches: The same pairing of girdle and battle garland yields lament in one poet and praise in the next, which shows that the thurai செருவிடை வீழ்தல் could be sung through the flower alone, with the warrior's death left wholly implicit.

note: Kural 774's hero sends his spear away with an elephant and laughs as he pulls one from his own body; 274's warrior hurls his spear at the oncoming elephant and, weaponless, takes the enemy's attack upon his body.
teaches: The Kural's couplet compresses a set scene that the Purananuru gives at length with dress and enemy horse, which shows that Valluvar's chapter on martial pride was built on stock battle episodes the audience already knew from heroic song.

note: Kural 69: the mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him (ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும்); 277: the old mother's joy at hearing her son died killing an elephant is greater than on the day she bore him (ஈன்ற ஞான்றினும் பெரிதே).
teaches: The Kural keeps the heroic measure of a mother's joy but moves its object from a son's death in battle to his being called worthy, so the pair shows Valluvar civilising a formula of the battlefield into one of learning and character.

note: Kural 69's mother rejoices on hearing her son praised; 278's mother hears a report of his flight, refuses it, searches the field, and rejoices more than at his birth only on seeing his body.
teaches: Where the Kural makes a mother's greatest joy depend on what she hears said of her son, 278 makes hearsay the thing to be refuted by sight of the wounds, which shows that the heroic mother trusted only the body's evidence of honour.

note: Both are உவகைக் கலுழ்ச்சி poems about an old mother whose son died in battle, and both end on joy greater than on the day she bore him (ஈன்ற ஞான்றினும் பெரிது).
teaches: One closing formula carries two different plots, joy at good news in 277 and joy after a false report of flight is disproved in 278, which shows that the thurai fixed the ending and left poets free to vary the path to it.

note: 312 lists the duties: to bear and rear the son is the mother's, to make him a warrior the father's, to kill elephants the son's; in 279 the father is already dead and the mother herself arms and dresses her only son for battle.
teaches: 312's tidy division of duties breaks down in 279, where the mother takes over the father's task of sending the son out because the men are dead, which shows the ideal of the warrior mother under the pressure of successive losses.

note: In 86 a mother says her womb is like a den a tiger has left and her son will be found on the battlefield; in 279 a mother with one son sends him to the battle after husband and kinsman have fallen.
teaches: 86 gives the mother's own proud voice and 279 an onlooker's awe at the same type, which shows that the warrior mother was praised both from within and from outside, and that the onlooker felt the cost (கெடுக சிந்தை) the mother does not speak.

note: 280's widows eat the seeds of the small white water lily (ஆம்பல் அல்லி உண்ணும்); 250's widow is the wife 'of lily-seed food' (அல்லி உணவின் மனைவி) with hair cut and bangles removed.
teaches: The repeated detail of lily-seed food in two poets shows that the widow's diet was a fixed public mark of her state, so that in 280 the wife can foretell her whole future by naming what she will eat.

teaches: Read together the two show the rite was done not only over a wound already seen but in anticipation, by every house in the village, so 296's anxiety is the same guarding as 281 started before the news has come.

teaches: The Kural's 'courage that has come down' is, in Avvaiyar, a three-generation bond between one fighting family and one royal family, so inherited courage meant inherited loyalty to a particular house.

teaches: Together they show the order of drinking as the measure of the order of dying: 290 asks for the first cup on the strength of the family's dead, 298 reads a poor cup as the loss of the vanguard.

teaches: Both turn a quarrel over drink into a claim to the front line, which shows the feast's order was read as a promise about the battle, and a warrior who seized one was claiming the other.

note: 294: no one approaches the warrior standing alone, as no one approaches the gem the serpent spits (அரவுஉமிழ் மணியின் குறுகார்); Kural 763: a host of rats roaring like the sea perish when the cobra breathes.
teaches: The Kural's cobra verse never mentions an army and its commentator reads it as one hero against a crowd; 294 uses the serpent exactly so, for a lone fighter in a confused battle whom the crowd will not approach, so the allegorical reading follows an image of the war poems.

note: 295: seeing her son broken in the battle press, his mother's dry breasts flow; Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him.
teaches: The Kural's mother hears praise and her joy exceeds the birth; Avvaiyar's mother sees the body and her breasts give milk as at the birth, so the Kural's comparison with childbirth has a harsher Sangam form in which the worth was proved by dying.

note: Both have the thurai உவகைக் கலுழ்ச்சி; in 278 a mother who swore to cut off the breast that fed him if he fled finds him dead facing the enemy; in 295 the mother's withered breasts flow on seeing his glory.
teaches: The two poems make the mother's breast the measure of the son's conduct, cut off for flight in 278 and filled again for his death in 295, so the thurai of joyful weeping has a fixed bodily sign.

note: 297 says it is right that cool fields (தண்ணடை) be given to speared warriors; 287 asks what getting cool fields is (தண்ணடை பெறுதல் யாவது?) to men who, if they die, enjoy the high world.
teaches: One poem claims the land grant as the warrior's due and the other waves it aside for heaven, so the war poems held two accounts of the hero's wage, and which one a poet used depended on whether he spoke for the living or the willing dead.

note: 299: the poor chief's gram-fed horse cleaves the front while the rich kings' ghee-fed horses hang back; Kural 769: an army wins if it is free of shrinking, lasting grievance and poverty (வறுமை).
teaches: The Kural counts poverty among the things that lose a war, while 299 makes the poor chief the winner and the rich the ones who shrink, so the Kural's rule is about an army's supply and the poem's point is that wealth does not supply courage.

note: 301's hero will lift his spear only against the king's mounted elephant (வேந்தூர் யானைக்கு அல்லது); Kural 772 prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare.
teaches: The Kural states the warrior's preference for a worthy target as a maxim of honour, and 301 shows the same preference working as a tactic, since the enemy camp is warned that a man who ignores lesser blows is saving himself for their king.

note: Both kuthirai maram poems name the young rider with one formula: நோக்கினர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (302) and எள்ளுநர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (303).
teaches: The epithet for the young horseman was a fixed frame with a free slot for his victims, those who look at him or those who mock him, so two poets of the same thurai shared a stock line and varied only whom it threatened.

note: 303's speaker killed an elephant yesterday and now waits for a young rider's spear in his chest; Kural 774's warrior sends his spear off with an elephant and laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: Both pair the elephant killed with the spear received, so the couplet's laughing warrior is the same type as 303's boaster, and the poem supplies the couplet's missing sequence: the elephant was yesterday, the wound is today's test.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one said is hard; in 304 the king's camp trembles because the hero's word is never two (இரண்டா காது அவன் கூறியது).
teaches: The Kural treats word and deed as a gap to be closed by effort, but 304 shows a man whose record has closed it so firmly that his spoken vow alone frightens an army, so keeping one's word becomes a weapon and not only a virtue.

note: Kural 685 says the envoy speaks briefly and brings good; 305's brahmin says only a few words (சொல்லிய சொல்லோ சிலவே) and the siege ladders and elephants' bells are put away.
teaches: The couplet's rule for the envoy, brevity that achieves its end, has a historical scene behind it in which the good brought was a war called off, and the poem credits that to the words' fewness rather than to the speaker's power.

note: Kural 81 says all household life is for receiving guests; 306's woman prays at the hero-stone first that she may have guests (விருந்து எதிர் பெறுகதில்) and then for her husband's war.
teaches: The Kural's claim that household life exists for guests was a prayer before it was a maxim: in 306 a warrior's wife asks the hero-stone for guests before she asks for her husband's victory, so hospitality ranked first even in a house that lived by war.

teaches: The Kural uses the battle hero as a simile for the family's mainstay, while 314 shows that in the warrior village they were literally the same man, so the couplet's comparison grew from a social fact that it turned into a figure.

note: Kural 490 says to fold up like the heron when it is time and strike like its beak when the moment comes; 315 says Anji can stay unseen like the fire-drill in the eaves and blaze like its fire when he appears.
teaches: Both reduce right timing to one object with two states, but Avvai's image puts the force inside the waiting thing (the fire is already in the stick), which adds to the couplet that restraint is stored strength rather than mere patience.

note: The idyll's rite offers rice mixed with a ram's blood and spreads millet with blood, and calls it worship that brings each seeker what he sought; Tirumular says that in worship the bright flower is not killing other small lives. teaches: The theme that the god cannot be measured, which Tirumular argues through the gods' failure, is already in the Sangam idyll as the suppliant's reason for coming to the feet, so unknowability led to approach rather than to despair from the start.

note: In the idyll the god appears in his own form to a living suppliant and says 'Fear not; I knew of your coming'; in the Thiruppugazh the poet asks that at the moment Death's servants come he appear on the peacock and end his fear.
teaches: The god's appearance and his word against fear, which the idyll promises to any suppliant who makes the journey, the later poet saves for the single hour of death, showing how the guide-poem's promise of a meeting became a plea for rescue.
